quiz.explanation: The notes explain that less resistant rock (such as clay) is eroded faster than more resistant rock (such as limestone), causing it to cave in and form a bay, while the resistant rock protrudes as a headland.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT listed in the notes as an erosional coastal feature?
quiz.explanation: The notes list erosional features as headlands and bays, wave-cut platforms, sea cliffs, sea caves/arches/stacks/stumps, and blowholes; bars are listed under depositional features instead.

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain how differential erosion leads to the formation of headlands and bays along a coastline, using the example given in the notes. [6]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Differential erosion occurs on coastlines made up of alternating bands of resistant rock, such as limestone and granite, and less resistant rock, such as sand, chalk and clay. As waves crash against the coast, hydraulic action and abrasion act more effectively on the less resistant rock, eroding it away at a faster rate than the more resistant rock nearby. Over time, with repeated and continuous erosion, this uneven attack causes the area of less resistant rock to be worn away and cave inward, forming wide indented curves known as bays, while the area of more resistant rock, having been eroded much less, remains protruding outward into the sea, forming headlands. This process of differential erosion is well illustrated along the Dorset Coast in England, where alternating rock resistance has produced a distinctive coastline of headlands and bays.
rubric: Explains the geological precondition (alternating resistant and less resistant rock bands)
Explains the mechanism of differential erosion (hydraulic action/abrasion acting more on less resistant rock)
Explains formation of bays (faster erosion of less resistant rock caving in) and headlands (slower erosion of resistant rock protruding)
References the named example (Dorset Coast, England) as required for support

shortAnswer.prompt: Suggest how wave refraction acts on a coastline of headlands and bays over time, and explain why this makes the coast a dynamic landform. [4]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Wave refraction is the process by which waves change direction as they approach an indented coastline of headlands and bays, and over time this process gradually works to straighten the coastline. This suggests that the coast is not a fixed or permanent landform, but a dynamic one that continues to change shape over time as a result of ongoing wave action, meaning the pronounced headlands and bays created by differential erosion will not remain in their current form indefinitely.
rubric: States that wave refraction changes wave direction as waves approach the indented coast
States that this process eventually acts to straighten the coastline
Explains why this shows the coast is dynamic (continually changing, not permanent)
Answer makes an inference/suggestion rather than simply restating the definition, as required by 'suggest'

topics.title: Wave Refraction: Headlands and Bays
topics.notesHtml:
Wave Refraction: Headlands and Bays

  • Coastlines with protruding headlands and inward-curving bays cause wave refraction: the headlands that protrude out act as an obstruction to the waves and disrupt the parallel pattern of the incoming waves, causing the waves to bend.
  • The obstruction posed by the headlands is the shallow water that the waves reach first, which causes the waves to slow down. Since one part of the wave is slowed down before the other part, the wave front becomes curved. This is called wave refraction. (Applies to sheltered coasts — a peninsula slows waves and protects bays or sheltered coasts, versus straight coasts, which have a long fetch and stronger erosion.)
  • When waves converge on the headlands, the wave energy is also more concentrated, giving rise to increased wave height and greater erosive energy at the headlands, forming notches, caves, wave-cut platforms and many other coastal landforms.
  • When the waves then go past the headlands and approach the bays, they approach the bay in a curved pattern, and as they diverge, the wave energy is also distributed and spread out, resulting in decreased wave height and reduced erosive energy, indicating more deposition, which often leads to the formation of beaches at the bay area.
  • With more erosion occurring at the headlands and more deposition occurring at the bay area, this eventually shortens the headlands and enlarges the bay. Over time, as the process of erosion and deposition repeatedly occurs, more erosion happens at the headlands due to the waves converging (resulting in higher wave energy), and more deposition happens at the bay area due to the waves dissipating (resulting in lower wave energy).
  • This causes the headlands to protrude out less and the bay to not curve inwards as much. Eventually, wave refraction ultimately results in the straightening of the coastline as the bay area becomes broader and bigger due to more deposition, and the headlands get shorter.

flashcards.q: What causes wave refraction at coastlines with headlands and bays?
flashcards.a: Headlands protrude out and act as an obstruction to waves, disrupting the parallel wave pattern and causing the waves to bend.

flashcards.q: Why do waves slow down first at headlands?
flashcards.a: Headlands are surrounded by shallow water, which the waves reach first, causing that part of the wave to slow down before the rest, curving the wave front.

flashcards.q: What happens to wave energy when waves converge on headlands?
flashcards.a: Wave energy becomes more concentrated, giving increased wave height and greater erosive energy.

flashcards.q: What landforms result from erosion at headlands due to wave convergence?
flashcards.a: Notches, caves, wave-cut platforms and other coastal landforms.

flashcards.q: What happens to wave energy as waves diverge approaching a bay?
flashcards.a: Wave energy is distributed and spread out, resulting in decreased wave height and reduced erosive energy.

flashcards.q: What landform commonly forms at bays due to wave divergence?
flashcards.a: Beaches, due to increased deposition.

flashcards.q: Over time, what happens to the headlands and bays as erosion and deposition continue?
flashcards.a: Headlands get shortened by erosion and bays get enlarged/broadened by deposition.

flashcards.q: What is the ultimate long-term result of wave refraction on a coastline?
flashcards.a: The straightening of the coastline, as the bay becomes broader/bigger and the headlands become shorter.

flashcards.q: What type of coast has a long fetch and stronger erosion, contrasted with a sheltered coast?
flashcards.a: A straight coast, as opposed to a sheltered coast where a peninsula slows waves and protects bays.

flashcards.q: What is a wave front?
flashcards.a: The leading edge of a wave; it becomes curved due to differential slowing of waves as they enter shallow water near headlands.

quiz.question: Why do waves bend (refract) around headlands?
choices: Longshore drift reverses direction at headlands
The headlands' shallow water slows part of the wave before the rest, curving the wave front
quiz.explanation: The notes state shallow water at headlands slows one part of the wave before the other, causing the wave front to curve.

quiz.question: What is the effect of wave convergence at headlands?
choices: Decreased wave height and reduced erosion
Increased wave height and greater erosive energy
quiz.explanation: Converging waves concentrate energy, increasing wave height and erosive power at headlands.

quiz.question: What typically forms at bays due to wave divergence?
quiz.explanation: Diverging waves lose energy, leading to deposition and beach formation at bays.

quiz.question: What is the long-term outcome of repeated erosion at headlands and deposition at bays?
quiz.explanation: Continued erosion shortens headlands while deposition enlarges bays, eventually straightening the coastline.

quiz.question: Which coast type experiences a long fetch and stronger erosion according to the notes?
quiz.explanation: The notes contrast sheltered coasts (protected by peninsulas) with straight coasts, which have long fetch and stronger erosion.

quiz.question: What landforms are associated with erosion at headlands?
quiz.explanation: The notes list notches, caves, wave-cut platforms as products of concentrated erosive energy at headlands.

quiz.question: How does wave height change at headlands compared to at bays, as waves converge and diverge respectively?
choices: Wave height decreases at headlands and increases at bays
Wave height stays the same at both headlands and bays
Wave height depends only on tidal range, not on refraction
Wave height increases at headlands (convergence) and decreases at bays (divergence)
quiz.explanation: The notes state that converging waves at headlands concentrate energy, increasing wave height and erosive energy, while diverging waves at bays spread energy out, decreasing wave height and erosive energy.

quiz.question: According to the notes, what coastline shape is required for wave refraction (bending) to occur?
choices: There must be no headlands present at all
The coastline must be indented and uneven, with headlands and bays disrupting the wave's parallel pattern
The seabed must be uniformly deep throughout
The coastline must be perfectly straight
quiz.explanation: The notes state that protruding headlands and inward-curving bays act as an obstruction that disrupts the parallel pattern of incoming waves, causing them to bend — this is wave refraction.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a consequence of wave refraction around headlands and bays, according to the notes?
choices: The bay becomes narrower and the headland grows longer over time
The coastline gradually straightens over a long period
Wave energy disperses at bays, favouring deposition
Wave energy concentrates at headlands, increasing erosion there
quiz.explanation: The notes state the opposite: erosion shortens the headlands while deposition enlarges/broadens the bays over time, eventually straightening the coastline — so a narrowing bay and lengthening headland is not a consequence described.

quiz.question: If wave refraction suddenly stopped occurring at a coastline with an existing headland and bay (e.g. waves began approaching perfectly parallel to the still-uneven coast), what would you expect based on the notes' description of the refraction process?
choices: The bay would suddenly turn into a new headland
Erosion at the headland and deposition at the bay would slow, since these are driven by the differential wave energy caused by refraction
Sea level would rise as a direct result
The coastline would erode uniformly and more rapidly everywhere
quiz.explanation: Since the notes attribute concentrated erosion at headlands and enhanced deposition at bays specifically to the convergence and divergence of wave energy caused by refraction, removing refraction would remove the mechanism driving this differential erosion and deposition.

shortAnswer.prompt: With reference to the process of wave refraction, explain why headlands experience greater erosion than bays. [4]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Headlands protrude out into the sea, so the shallow water surrounding them is reached first by incoming waves, slowing that part of the wave down before the rest and causing the wave front to curve (refract). As waves converge on the headland due to this refraction, wave energy becomes concentrated, resulting in increased wave height and greater erosive energy. This concentrated energy erodes the headland through processes forming notches, caves and wave-cut platforms. In contrast, as waves pass the headland and diverge towards the bay, wave energy is spread out, reducing wave height and erosive energy, so the headland experiences far more erosion than the bay.
rubric: States that headlands are obstructions surrounded by shallow water, causing waves to slow and refract
Explains that wave convergence at headlands concentrates energy, increasing wave height and erosive power
Names resulting landforms (notches, caves, wave-cut platforms) at headlands
Contrasts with divergence and reduced energy at bays to show why erosion is greater at headlands
Answer begins with a general statement and ends with a concluding link back to the question

shortAnswer.prompt: Describe how a coastline with alternating headlands and bays changes over time as a result of wave refraction. [4]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Over time, due to wave refraction, headlands undergo continuous erosion from concentrated wave energy, gradually being shortened, while bays experience continuous deposition from dissipated wave energy, gradually being enlarged and broadened, often forming beaches. As this repeated cycle of erosion at headlands and deposition at bays continues, the headlands protrude less and the bays curve inward less, until eventually the coastline straightens out.
rubric: Describes headlands shortening due to erosion from concentrated wave energy
Describes bays broadening/enlarging due to deposition from dissipated wave energy
Notes the process repeats over time
States the eventual outcome: straightening of the coastline

topics.title: Wave-Cut Platform (Caves and Notches)
topics.notesHtml:
Wave-Cut Platform (+ Caves and Notches)

  • When destructive waves crash against the rock face between its high and low tide, the base of the cliff is eroded through hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution, concentrated at the cracks and lines of weaknesses at the base.
  • As a result, the base of the cliff will gradually erode, and over time, with the repetition of this process enlarging the crack and weakening the base, a notch (or wave-cut notch) is formed.
  • As erosion proceeds over a longer period of time, as the waves continually crash against the rock face between its high and low tide, the wave-cut notch is deeply undercut and enlarged to form an overhang — the piece of rock above the notch — and subsequently a cave.
  • Over time, when further erosion causes the notch to become deeper and the overhang along with the cave to be larger, due to gravity, the roof of the cave loses support, it collapses, and a cliff is formed.
  • Further undercutting at the base of the cliff forms an overhanging portion which eventually collapses as well.
  • As the steep cliff retreats landwards, a gently sloping rocky platform between the base of the cliff and low tide level is formed, called a wave-cut platform.
  • Example: A wave-cut platform is found at Flamborough Head in Yorkshire, England.
  • Over time, an extended wave-cut platform can form as cliff profiles vary greatly, depending on: 1) rate of coastal erosion (cliff retreat), 2) strength of the rock, 3) presence of joints and bedding planes.
  • The wave-cut platform is covered with rock fragments from the receding cliff. Rocks being carried forward and backward by breakers smoothen the wave-cut platform by abrasion.
  • As the wave-cut platform lengthens, wave attack at the base of the cliff is reduced. Weathering and mass wasting (downhill movement of loosened and broken materials owing to gravity) become more important than marine erosion.

flashcards.q: What processes erode the base of a cliff at high and low tide?
flashcards.a: Hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution, concentrated at cracks and lines of weakness.

flashcards.q: What is a notch (wave-cut notch)?
flashcards.a: A gradually eroded indentation at the base of a cliff formed as cracks are enlarged and weakened over time.

flashcards.q: How does a cave form from a notch?
flashcards.a: Continued erosion deeply undercuts and enlarges the notch, forming an overhang and then a cave.

flashcards.q: Why does a cliff eventually collapse?
flashcards.a: Further erosion deepens the notch and enlarges the overhang/cave until the roof loses support due to gravity and collapses.

flashcards.q: What forms after the cliff face collapses and retreats landward?
flashcards.a: A gently sloping rocky platform between the base of the cliff and low tide level, called a wave-cut platform.

flashcards.q: Give an example location of a wave-cut platform.
flashcards.a: Flamborough Head in Yorkshire, England.

flashcards.q: What three factors affect the variation of cliff profiles over time?
flashcards.a: Rate of coastal erosion (cliff retreat), strength of the rock, and presence of joints and bedding planes.

flashcards.q: How is the wave-cut platform smoothened over time?
flashcards.a: Rock fragments from the receding cliff are carried forward and backward by breakers, smoothing the platform by abrasion.

flashcards.q: What happens to wave attack as the wave-cut platform lengthens?
flashcards.a: Wave attack at the base of the cliff is reduced.

flashcards.q: What becomes more important than marine erosion once the wave-cut platform lengthens?
flashcards.a: Weathering and mass wasting (downhill movement of loosened and broken materials owing to gravity).

quiz.question: What erosional processes act at the base of a cliff to form a notch?
choices: Hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution
quiz.explanation: The notes state these four processes, concentrated at cracks and weaknesses, erode the cliff base to form a notch.

quiz.question: What causes a cliff to eventually collapse and retreat?
choices: The overhang above the enlarged notch and cave loses support due to gravity
Rising sea levels flood the cliff

quiz.question: What is a wave-cut platform?

An underwater trench formed by erosion
quiz.explanation: The notes define the wave-cut platform as the gently sloping rocky platform left as the cliff retreats.

quiz.question: Which location is given as an example of a wave-cut platform?
quiz.explanation: Flamborough Head in Yorkshire is explicitly named as an example location.

quiz.question: What smoothens the wave-cut platform over time?

quiz.question: What three factors cause cliff profiles to vary greatly?
choices: Rate of coastal erosion, rock strength, presence of joints/bedding planes

quiz.explanation: The notes list these three factors as reasons for variation in cliff profiles.

quiz.question: What is mass wasting, as defined in the notes?
choices: The chemical dissolving of limestone by seawater

The vertical rise and fall of tides
The horizontal movement of waves along the coast
quiz.explanation: The notes define mass wasting as 'the downhill movement of loosened and broken materials owing to gravity', which becomes more important than marine erosion once a wave-cut platform lengthens.

quiz.question: What happens to the wave-cut notch as erosion continues over a longer period of time?
choices: It fills up with sediment and disappears
It is undercut and enlarged to form an overhang, and subsequently a cave
It turns directly into a wave-cut platform without further change
quiz.explanation: The notes state that as erosion proceeds, 'the wave-cut notch is deeply undercut and enlarged to form an overhang... and subsequently a cave.'

quiz.question: Why does marine (wave) erosion become less important relative to weathering and mass wasting as a wave-cut platform lengthens?
choices: A longer platform reduces wave attack at the base of the cliff
Cliffs stop retreating once any platform forms
Longer platforms increase wave height, increasing erosion further
Weathering only occurs after the platform disappears completely
quiz.explanation: The notes state that 'as the wave-cut platform lengthens, wave attack at the base of the cliff is reduced,' so weathering and mass wasting become more important than marine erosion.

quiz.question: Based on the sequence described in the notes, what is the correct order of formation, from earliest to latest: notch, overhang, cave, cliff collapse and retreat?
choices: Notch → Overhang → Cave → Cliff collapse and retreat
Overhang → Notch → Cliff collapse and retreat → Cave
Cave → Notch → Overhang → Cliff collapse and retreat
Notch → Cave → Cliff collapse and retreat → Overhang
quiz.explanation: The notes describe the sequence as: a notch forms at the cliff base, which is undercut and enlarged into an overhang and then a cave, until the cave's roof loses support and collapses, causing the cliff to retreat landwards.

quiz.question: Hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution all act together at a cliff. According to the notes, why does the notch specifically form at the base of the cliff rather than higher up?
choices: Because the top of the cliff is made of more resistant rock everywhere
Because solution/corrosion cannot occur at sea level
Because attrition only occurs above the high tide mark
Because destructive wave action and erosion processes are concentrated at the base, between high and low tide
quiz.explanation: The notes state that 'when destructive waves crash against the rock face between its high and low tide, the base of the cliff is eroded' through hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution, concentrated at that location.

shortAnswer.prompt: With the aid of a well-labelled diagram, explain the formation of a wave-cut platform. [6]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Destructive waves crash against the rock face between high and low tide, eroding the base of the cliff through hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution, concentrated at cracks and lines of weakness (1). This repeated erosion enlarges the crack, forming a wave-cut notch (2). Continued erosion undercuts and enlarges the notch further, forming an overhang and eventually a cave (3). As erosion continues, the notch deepens and the cave/overhang enlarges until the overhanging rock loses support due to gravity and collapses, forming a steep cliff (4). Further undercutting at the new cliff base causes repeated collapse, and as the cliff retreats landward, a gently sloping rocky platform is left between the base of the cliff and the low tide level – the wave-cut platform (5). Over time, rock fragments carried by breakers smoothen this platform by abrasion, and as the platform lengthens, wave attack on the cliff base is reduced, so weathering and mass wasting become more important than marine erosion.
rubric: Diagram/sketch showing labelled stages: notch, cave, overhang, cliff collapse, wave-cut platform

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain why cliff profiles vary greatly along different stretches of coastline. [4]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Cliff profiles vary due to differences in the rate of coastal erosion (cliff retreat) between locations, the strength of the underlying rock (harder rock erodes more slowly and forms steeper cliffs), and the presence of joints and bedding planes which create lines of weakness that are more easily eroded. These factors interact differently at each location, causing cliff shapes and retreat rates to differ.

topics.title: River and Coastal Protection Measures: Overview
topics.notesHtml:
River and Coastal Protection Measures

As a result of erosion and the effects of processes along the river and the coast, there is a need for river and/or coastal protection measures. These measures have their pros and cons and can be classified into two categories: soft and hard engineering measures.

  • Hard engineering measures are defined as short term, more expensive, less sustainable measures with a greater impact on the river landscape and surrounding environment. They require more extensive alterations to the river to try to stop flooding.
  • Soft engineering measures are defined as long term, less expensive, more sustainable and ecologically sensitive measures with a low impact on the environment, aiming to protect the coasts from physical processes while still allowing them to take place. They attempt to manage the flood rather than prevent it.

flashcards.q: Why are river and coastal protection measures needed?
flashcards.a: As a result of erosion and the effects of processes along rivers and coasts, protection is needed to manage impacts.

flashcards.q: Into what two categories can protection measures be classified?
flashcards.a: Soft engineering measures and hard engineering measures.

flashcards.q: What defines hard engineering measures?
flashcards.a: Short term, more expensive, less sustainable measures with a greater impact on the landscape and environment, requiring extensive alterations.

flashcards.a: Long term, less expensive, more sustainable and ecologically sensitive measures with low environmental impact.

flashcards.a: No, they aim to protect the coasts while still allowing physical processes to take place.

flashcards.q: What is the aim of soft engineering measures regarding flooding?
flashcards.a: They attempt to manage the flood rather than prevent it.

flashcards.q: What is the aim of hard engineering measures regarding flooding?
flashcards.a: They try to stop flooding through extensive alterations to the river/coast.

flashcards.q: Which type of measure generally has a lower cost?

shortAnswer.prompt: Compare hard and soft engineering measures used to protect rivers and coasts. [6]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Hard and soft engineering measures share the common purpose of protecting rivers and coasts from the effects of erosion and flooding. However, they differ significantly. Hard engineering measures are short term, more expensive, and less sustainable, requiring extensive alterations to the river or coast that have a greater impact on the landscape and surrounding environment, aiming to stop flooding/erosion outright. In contrast, soft engineering measures are long term, less expensive, more sustainable and ecologically sensitive, having a low impact on the environment while still allowing natural physical processes to take place; rather than preventing floods, they attempt to manage them. Thus while both aim to protect against erosion/flooding, hard measures prioritise immediate, forceful prevention at higher cost and environmental impact, whereas soft measures prioritise long-term sustainability by working with natural processes.

topics.title: Soft Coastal Protection Measures
topics.notesHtml:
Soft Coastal Protection Measures

1. Beach Nourishment

Beach nourishment is a soft engineering measure which builds up the beach by replenishing beach material, particularly at the base of a structure, to provide a "natural" solution to absorbing wave energy. The process involves continually replacing lost beach material (like sand lost by coastal erosion or longshore drift) from a natural store either offshore (beach rebuilding) or from downshore along a stretch of longshore drift (beach recycling).

Examples: Vale do Lobo Beach, Portugal; Cancún, Mexico; Gold Coast, Australia.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Does not disrupt the beach's physical appearance (blends in with existing beach); aesthetically better solution (natural looking — difficult to tell that management is taking place)
Beach does not shrink in size, allowing tourists to continue to use the beach (larger beaches appeal to tourists)
Provides most "natural" solution		Sand may erode
Can be expensive to keep transporting large amounts of sand (sediment will be moved by longshore drift so it will need frequent replenishment unless other defences are used) and has to be repeated periodically (may accumulate high costs over time)
Beach is inaccessible during nourishment

2. Sand Dune Stabilisation

Sand dunes are a natural feature and are ridges of sand along the coast. Sand dune stabilisation involves the use of vegetation, like the growth of spinifex and marram grass, or sand fencing to trap sand and stabilise the sand dune, preventing the dunes from shifting along the coast and preventing erosion of sand dunes.

Examples: Bei Men Coast; Bondi Beach, Australia; Dune de Pyla, Southwestern Coast of France; Francois Peron Natural Park, Australia.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Creates new habitats for wildlife
Creates opportunities for nature studies
Blends in with the natural surrounding, maintaining a natural looking coastline
Prevents flooding of inland areas and the coast
Relatively cheap
Sand dunes protect coastal deposition and human features like houses and roads against coastal erosion		Reduces area of the beach accessible to the public (may take away tourism from the beach)
Can be damaged by storm waves
Sand dunes can migrate landwards and destroy property and roads
Vegetation on dunes can be destroyed by human activities — hiking, recreational activities

3. Managed Retreat/Realignment

Instead of preventing erosion or flooding, managed retreat/realignment allows these processes to happen naturally, allowing the beaches to become marshes, marshlands, or wetlands. These can then help to prevent erosion of the beach — for example, marshlands bring about vegetation that can help to stabilise sediment and reduce the speed and energy of the waves, reducing their erosive power.

Examples: Abereiddy, Pembrokeshire; Marshes East of the Kalahari Desert in Okavango Delta, Botswana; Medmerry, Sussex, UK; Abbotts Hall, Essex, UK.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Most cost effective and most environmentally friendly
Creates new habitats for wildlife
Marshes formed as a result can help to slow down waves and reduce erosion as a natural defence		Loss of land (homes and farmhouses) — people may need to be compensated for lost buildings or farmland (high cost of compensation)
Limited to non-built-up areas, reducing efficiency
Unwillingness from inhabitants, restricting implementation

4. Cliff Stabilisation

Cliff stabilisation involves reducing the slope angle of the cliff and planting vegetation to reduce erosion.

Example: Mappleton, Holderness Coast.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Prevents erosion of valuable land and maintains the current coastline by reducing erosion
Cliff becomes more stable and is less prone to unexpected movement		May be impractical if valuable land exists on the cliff
High maintenance costs

5. Planting Mangroves Along the Coast

Mangroves are vegetation adapted to a muddy coast. The 2004 tsunami proved the effectiveness of mangroves in protecting coastal regions.

Example: In 2005, the Malaysian government launched a project to plant mangroves to protect 4800 km of coastal lands.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
The roots of the trees anchor them firmly to the mud, preventing waves from eroding it
Mangroves form a buffer zone, reducing the erosional impact of waves and wind		Difficult to establish mangroves as young plants are fragile
The programme requires the cooperation of local people to protect saplings against animals and human activities

6. Encouraging Growth of Coral Reefs

Coral reefs are clusters of rock-like substances called coral. They often grow in shallow seas near the coast.

Examples: In Malaysia, the government encouraged growth of coral reefs by banning fishing and pollution. In Singapore, the government is also trying to grow coral reefs artificially.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Coral reefs make the sea shallow, slowing down the speed of waves, so waves have less energy to erode the coast
Natural solution that may also be an attraction for tourist snorkelers or divers		Human activities (e.g. dynamite fishing, sand mining, land reclamation, pollution) have destroyed corals
Difficult to maintain as it requires the cooperation of many groups of people, like fishermen and governments

shortAnswer.prompt: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of using beach nourishment as a coastal protection measure. [4]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Beach nourishment has several advantages: it does not disrupt the beach's physical appearance, blending in naturally and appearing aesthetically better than hard structures; it keeps the beach large enough for tourists to continue using it; and it provides the most natural-looking solution among coastal defences. However, it also has disadvantages: the sand may erode again due to longshore drift, meaning it can be expensive to keep transporting sand and the process has to be repeated periodically, accumulating high costs over time; additionally, the beach becomes inaccessible during the nourishment process itself.

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain how mangroves and coral reefs act as natural (soft) measures to protect coastlines from erosion. [6]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Mangroves are vegetation adapted to muddy coasts whose roots anchor firmly into the mud, preventing waves from eroding it, and they form a buffer zone that reduces the erosional impact of waves and wind on the coast behind them; for example, in 2005 the Malaysian government launched a project to plant mangroves to protect 4800 km of coastal lands. Coral reefs, meanwhile, are rock-like clusters that grow in shallow seas near the coast; their presence makes the sea shallower, slowing down the speed of incoming waves so that they carry less energy and thus erode the coast less, and in Malaysia the government encouraged coral growth by banning fishing and pollution. Both measures work by dissipating wave energy naturally before it reaches the shore, rather than blocking waves with hard structures, but both face the disadvantage of being fragile and difficult to establish or maintain, requiring cooperation from local communities and protection from human activities such as dynamite fishing or animal disturbance.

topics.title: Hard Coastal Protection Measures
topics.notesHtml:
Hard Coastal Protection Measures

1. Seawall

A seawall is a concrete wall, curved on the seaward side to deflect the power of the waves. They block the waves and reflect the energy back into the sea, preventing flooding of the land and structures behind it, and protecting areas of human habitation, conservation, and tourism or leisure activities from wave or tidal action.

Examples: Stanley Park, Vancouver; Ventnor on the Isle of Wight, England; Urangan, Queensland; Paravur near Kollam City in India; Galveston Island, Texas; Omaha Beach, New Zealand.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Protects the base of cliffs and protects beaches and coasts from erosion
Prevents coastal flooding
Reduces the energy and impact of the waves greatly and is very effective in protecting the coast from erosion
Sea walls reflect rather than absorb wave energy, meaning it is one of the most effective means of preventing erosion		Most expensive to build and maintain (up to 2.5 billion pounds/km), average lifespan of only 75 years before they must be replaced
Unattractive, affecting the landscape of the coast, and may also cause ecological damage as it intrudes into the coast
Curved sea walls merely reflect the energy of the waves back to the sea and do not necessarily reduce the energy of the waves in all cases
Deflected waves often scour the base, undermining the wall (may eventually collapse)

2. Revetments

Revetments are wooden or steel structures which break the force of the waves and trap beach material behind them. They prevent existing beaches from getting washed away and may contribute to beach building, by reducing wave action at the boundary between the sea and land.

Examples: Dynamic revetment at Cape Lookout State Park, Oregon; Colhugh Beach, Llantwit Major, Wales; Norfolk, UK.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Much cheaper than a sea wall and most hard engineering measures, and effective for many years
Absorbs wave energy through the slats
Can be made permeable or impermeable, resulting in increased effectiveness of dissipating the force of waves
Rather effective at breaking the force of the waves		Expensive (approximately 1000 pounds per metre) and may simply displace erosion to other non-protected, downdrift areas
Less durable than a sea wall, hence may need regular maintenance many times, and is not effective in stormy conditions; does not give total protection to the base of the cliff
Requires large space
Environmentally ugly, unattractive

3. Groynes

Groynes are barriers built at right angles to the coastline, made of wood or (in some cases) steel. They prevent existing beaches from getting washed away by longshore drift, acting as a physical barrier that interrupts wave action and intercepts sand moving along the shore, accumulating this sand against the updrift side of the structure and building the beach. However, this also leaves the downdrift side of the beach deprived of sand, resulting in erosion there.

Examples: UK Flood Act of 2010; Gold Coast and East Coast, Australia.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Encourages and allows the build-up of a beach — beaches are a natural defence against erosion and an attraction for tourists
Stops and prevents longshore drift moving beach material along the coast, effectively reducing erosion		Can be unattractive
Costly to build and maintain (approximately 5000 to 6000 pounds each)
May not be the most effective as it cannot prevent the significant cross-shore erosion that typically occurs during storms
Results in the depletion of sand on the downdrift side of the beach, making that area more susceptible to erosion — merely transferring erosion further along the beach rather than resolving the problem
Can increase erosion further down the coast by stopping longshore drift and starving areas further down coast of sediment

4. Riprap

Ripraps are piles of large boulders placed along the coastline that are interlocked together, with the purpose of dissipating wave energy. They also have gaps which lessen the force of the waves by absorbing wave energy within the gaps between the rocks, allowing them to break down and weaken. They also prevent existing beaches from getting washed away and may contribute to beach building.

Example: San Francisco Bay.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Easy to maintain
Durable and long lasting
Relatively cheap as compared to other measures as it uses natural materials/rocks		More expensive than vegetated slopes
Does not provide the habitat enhancement that vegetative practices do
Not effective in stormy conditions
Environmentally ugly and may be unattractive
Can be undermined and removed by waves due to washing away of sand and shingle beneath

5. Tetrapods

Tetrapods are typically 4-pronged concrete structures placed on shorelines which help to dissipate energy from waves and reinforce other coastal structures. They are often arranged in interlocking positions, and waves are allowed to flow around and between them, reducing wave reflection and backwash and reducing erosion to the tetrapods themselves.

Examples: Sendai Coast, Japan; Crescent City, California.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Pre-casted (cast into their final shape before being positioned), hence can be placed swiftly when waves are incoming
Successful in reducing coastal erosion by many tsunamis at Crescent City, California, USA
Strong, durable structures		Very costly to build and pose a threat to swimmers, surfers, boaters and recreational fishermen
An eyesore along the beach
Expensive to construct

6. Breakwaters

Breakwaters are structures constructed near the coasts, typically arranged parallel to the coast and usually made of granite. They create a zone of shallow water between themselves and the coast, designed as part of coastal management or to protect an anchorage from the effects of both weather and longshore drift.

Examples: East Coast Park and Siloso Beach, Sentosa, Singapore.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Does not interfere with the flow of water
Waves break on the seaward face of the breakwater, creating calm waters behind it which encourage deposition of sediments, creating beaches		Expensive and a permanent feature like most hard engineering, meaning it is a long-term modification to the shoreline
Cannot provide complete protection of the coast — unprotected areas are prone to erosion

7. Gabions

Gabions are cages of boulders built into the cliff face, and the small rocks help to absorb the wave energy.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Effective where erosion is severe, and cheaper than sea wallsEnvironmentally ugly (usually used in large numbers)
High cost of approximately 350 pounds per metre

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain why groynes, despite being effective at building up beaches, can create problems elsewhere along the coast. [4]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Groynes are barriers built at right angles to the coastline that intercept sand moving along the shore due to longshore drift, causing sand to accumulate against the updrift side of the structure and build up the beach there, which is beneficial as beaches act as a natural defence against erosion and attract tourists. However, because groynes intercept the longshore drift of sand, the downdrift side of the beach is left deprived of sediment, making that area more susceptible to erosion. This means groynes do not solve the erosion problem but merely transfer it further along the coast to unprotected areas, which is a significant limitation of this hard engineering measure.
rubric: Explains how groynes trap sand via interception of longshore drift on the updrift side
States the resulting benefit (beach build-up, tourist draw, erosion defence)
Explains the downdrift side is starved of sediment and becomes more prone to erosion
Concludes that groynes displace rather than solve the erosion problem

shortAnswer.prompt: Compare seawalls and breakwaters as hard coastal protection measures. [6]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Both seawalls and breakwaters are hard engineering measures designed to protect the coast from wave erosion and are costly, permanent structures with environmental impact. However, they differ in design and function: seawalls are curved concrete walls built directly on the shoreline that block and reflect wave energy back into the sea, preventing coastal flooding but potentially causing scouring at their base as deflected waves undermine them. Breakwaters, in contrast, are structures built parallel to and offshore from the coast, creating a zone of shallow, calm water between themselves and the coast; rather than reflecting all wave energy, they allow waves to break on their seaward face, encouraging deposition of sediment and the formation of beaches behind them. Thus, while seawalls directly wall off the land from wave attack, breakwaters work by calming the water further out to sea to encourage natural beach building, though both remain expensive, long-term coastal modifications that cannot guarantee complete protection.
rubric: States the common purpose (both hard, costly, protect against erosion)
Describes seawall function/location (on the shoreline, reflects wave energy)
Describes breakwater function/location (offshore, parallel, creates calm water for deposition)
Compares them generally rather than only listing one
Concludes noting shared limitations (cost, cannot fully prevent erosion)

topics.title: Soft River Protection Measures
topics.notesHtml:
Soft River Protection Measures

1. Planting Vegetation

Increasing the number of trees planted around the river valley, like replanting forests or planting new forests, allows for more infiltration and interception, reducing surface runoff and lowering the risks of floods.

Examples: Boscastle, Cornwall, UK; Afon Tywi, Carmarthenshire; Green Belt Movement (Kenya).

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Economic benefits (forestry)
Provides new ecosystems, benefits environment
Relatively low cost option, which enhances environmental quality of the drainage basin
Less water gets to the river, reducing the discharge
The ecosystem of the area is protected
Very effective method for reducing discharge, while keeping the environment protected		Cannot fully prevent flooding, only reduces the likelihood
Reduces farmland
Difficult to plant forests in urban areas
Takes time for the flood prevention to be successful

2. Sustainable Drainage

Filter strips and permeable paving allow for more infiltration into the ground. Sustainable drainage results in a lower amount of water that would directly flow into the river channel, as there is more throughflow and groundwater flow, which is much slower compared to surface runoff (which carries only a low amount of water).

However, it has disadvantages such as the high cost of the measure, as engineers have to factor in creating impermeable pathways to increase surface runoff. Older buildings might also not be able to have this function.

Example: UK Flood Act of 2010.

3. Washlands

Washlands involve setting aside areas of land of lower importance where water can wash during a flood, to be flooded when river levels get too high, usually at the lower course of the river. Flood gates can let water flood this area easily, diverting it away from more densely populated and more important areas.

Examples: Yangtze River, China, Jingjiang Basin; The Ouse Washes of Cambridgeshire.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Easy to construct; only requires sluice gates
Land is often available for use most of the time as an empty lot and can be used for other purposes (farming, residential); water is only allowed in when major floods are imminent
Easily manages and controls floods with less need to construct hard engineering
Cheap and rather effective		May become silted due to farming, causing them to become unsuitable for use (if not maintained properly)
People living in washlands have to be evacuated during major floods
Hard to find such an available place

4. Land-Use Zoning/Floodplain Zoning

Land-use or floodplain zoning involves dividing settlements and areas into different levels of flood risk: red for areas likely to experience a high degree of flooding, yellow for areas where flooding is possible but unlikely, and green for areas where it is very unlikely to take place. The urban land use areas are zoned to reduce the flood risk impacts.

Example: Yangtze River, China, Jingjiang Basin.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Helps influence planners to decide where certain settlements should be located to minimise the cost and damages incurred should a flood occur
Buildings and land that are expensive to insure are located further away from the river
Areas next to the river are able to flood, as they are zoned as green places/farmland
Less claims for insurance, as businesses and houses are not flooded		Difficult to allocate land and change existing land uses
Does not prevent the flood from occurring, only minimises its effect
Not always possible to develop old urban areas into new zones
Some people might not approve of the zoning methods
Can take time to zone the area next to the river
It does not stop the flood

5. Flood Warning Systems/Flood Warning and Preparation

Flood control monitoring systems detect risks of floods, and communication networks relay warnings to people in high-risk zones, allowing them to save their possessions and evacuate with their lives. Warnings can be given via newspaper, TV, radio, and the internet.

Example: Yangtze River, China, Jingjiang Basin.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Saves many lives by providing warnings to evacuate prior to the flood
Requires very little modification or construction around the river
People know when to protect their houses with methods such as sandbags and when to leave
People can have their houses and businesses insured		Requires advanced technology; high cost
Does not prevent property or infrastructure damage
May be ineffective during flash floods as there is not enough time to react
Not all people have access to the methods of warning, especially in rural areas, making this method less accessible for rural dwellers
Not all insurance companies will insure people who have buildings near a known flooded area
Some flash floods can be too quick for the warning systems to be effective
Does not stop the flood

topics.title: Hard River Protection Measures
topics.notesHtml:
Hard River Protection Measures

1. Flood Barriers

Flood barriers act as gates in the river that can be activated to prevent a large surge in river discharge during a storm, preventing floods from occurring. They can be used to raise the height of the river bank to a level where the river will not burst its banks.

Examples: Maeslant Barrier in the Netherlands; River Thames in London; Delta Works in the Netherlands; St. Petersburg Dam in Finland; glass barriers in use in Keswick, Cumbria.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Can be activated only when necessary, meaning it can be temporary and non-obstructive most of the time
Can be a permanent feature or a feature incorporated into the design of an area (does not look unnatural or unattractive, does not largely affect the appearance of the landscape)		Expensive with high cost and requires advanced technology
Consumes/requires large space
May have an environmental impact on river wildlife

2. Dredging

As deposition occurs, silt builds up on the river bed over time. During heavy rain, due to this accumulation of silt, river discharge spills over its banks and floods the surrounding area. Using excavators or pumps to remove this silt allows for larger river capacity and faster flow downstream, reducing the risk of floods. Dredging the bottom of the river for sediment means the river is deeper and can hold more water.

Examples: River Tone and Parrett in Somerset, UK; Netherlands.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
River can hold more water, reducing flood risk in the built-up area
Allows river to be used as a shipping route
Easy method to reduce flooding in built-up areas		Has to be done frequently to ensure effectiveness (expensive and may accumulate high costs over time)
Increases river velocity, which may lead to flooding at the lower course
Can change the ecosystem in the river

3. Levees/Embankments

Levees are concrete or wooden walls that hold back the river from the banks. They raise the banks of a river and prevent water from spilling over, containing the discharge during a storm, thus reducing the risk of flooding.

Examples: Yangtze River in Hubei, China; Moskva River in Moscow; Delta Works in the Netherlands.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Allows for more flood water to be contained within the river, reducing flood risk in the built-up area
Cheaper as it is only a one-time construction/one-off cost
Lower environmental impact; may 'blend in' to the environmental landscape; doesn't destroy animal habitats
More water can pass through
Banks will not erode, protecting land next to the river
Only needs to be built once and then maintained, so relatively cheap		May appear unattractive/unnatural (if concrete)
Increases river velocity, which may lead to flooding at the lower course
Limited protection as they cannot reach very high
Prone to breaking during major floods
Velocity of water can increase, increasing flood risk further downstream
Looks unnatural, which some might not like

4. Dams

Dams are concrete and steel structures built along the course of a river to control the amount of discharge. Dams trap and hold back water from the river, building up a reservoir which can release water in a controlled way.

Examples: Yangtze River, Sandouping Town, Yiling; Three Gorges Dam in China; Marina Barrage in Singapore; Hoover Dam, Nevada, US.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Tourist attraction
Can be used to produce electricity by flowing water through a hydro-electric turbine
Controls river flooding more than any other method
Major dams can protect millions of lives
Improves safety and transport throughout the river
Reservoirs act as a water source		Habitats around the dam are flooded, which can destroy ecosystems and vegetation, and result in rotting vegetation that releases methane (a GHG) into the air
Increased water pressure on walls of dams may increase incidence of earthquakes
Building the dam displaces many people, destroying settlements and farmlands (especially in developing countries where locals are not always consulted and have little say in where they are relocated)
Sediments accumulate at the dam, reducing the volume of water the river can hold
Requires large space and is very expensive

5. Straightening and Deepening/Diversion Spillways

Widening or deepening the river channel increases its capacity and allows it to hold more discharge. A straighter river also allows water to travel faster downstream, diverting it away from settlements. Artificial channels known as diversion spillways can also divert water away from areas at particular risk of flooding, sending it back into the river further downstream.

Examples: Boscastle, Cornwall, UK; Spillway on River Wyre.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Water is able to move out of the area faster because it doesn't travel as far
Allows river to be used as a shipping route
High degree of control over the flow of water		Increases flooding and may lead to greater erosion downstream in the lower courses
Spoils the natural look of the area or changes the ecosystem there
Areas close to where the spillway rejoins the river are at greater risk of flooding due to increased discharge

6. Channelisation

Direct channelisation involves straightening and reinforcing the beds and banks, for the purpose of allowing water to pass through quicker due to the lack of friction, reducing the risk of flooding and preventing erosion.

Example: Los Angeles River, USA.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Reduces friction and increases velocity of river
Bank erosion is greatly reduced
Water will go through the river quickly, reducing the risk of flooding
River channel can hold more water		Costly
Not natural, so it is harder for vegetation and wildlife to survive
Velocity of the water can increase, increasing risk of flooding further downstream
As sediment builds up over time, dredging needs to be done frequently

topics.title: Evaluation of Hard and Soft Engineering Measures
topics.notesHtml:
Evaluation

Both hard and soft engineering measures are equally important. However, their importance and effectiveness vary and can be looked at from different concepts.

  • Place — Different places have different coastlines and rivers, shaped differently, some with steeper gradients and some with gentler gradients, with different kinds of landscapes, landforms and uses. This influences the ability for engineering measures to be implemented, considering their different disadvantages. For example, why does Hong Kong implement tetrapods at their coast whereas Singapore uses breakwaters? This could be due to the fact that tetrapods are too massive and large for Singapore's coastlines and pose a risk to beach goers.
  • Power and Place — All these measures cost money, and just like with other measures (e.g. earthquake measures), the ability to implement such measures and the choice of measures ultimately depend on the government and the resources they have. For less economically developed countries, it may be harder to implement hard measures due to a lack of resources, whereas more economically developed countries, with expertise, technology and financial resources, find it much easier. This is similar to mitigation and adaptation: mitigation is like hard engineering measures, while adaptation is like soft engineering measures. Just as less economically developed countries are unable to mitigate and have to adapt, they are unable to implement hard engineering measures and have to adopt soft ones instead.

Ultimately, it would be ideal for hard engineering measures to be implemented first, and then for soft engineering measures to be implemented to sustain it in the long run, since both are equally important. It is also important to weigh both of them in different circumstances alongside their limitations. Hard engineering measures are more drastic and have a larger impact, though they are hard to implement, facing limitations such as cost, unsightliness and the risks they pose. Soft engineering measures have a much smaller impact, though they may be easier to implement and are more long lasting for the long term.

shortAnswer.prompt: To what extent do you agree that hard engineering measures are more effective than soft engineering measures in protecting coasts and rivers? [10]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: This statement can be agreed to a moderate extent, as hard engineering measures often provide more immediate and drastic protection against erosion and flooding, but soft engineering measures offer more sustainable long-term benefits, meaning neither can be considered unconditionally superior. On one hand, hard engineering measures have a larger, more immediate impact in protecting against erosion and flooding, as they involve extensive structural alterations (e.g. sea walls, dams) capable of directly blocking or containing destructive forces; this makes them particularly effective in the short term and in areas of high economic value where immediate protection is critical. However, hard measures are costly, often unsustainable, and can create new problems, such as groynes starving downdrift beaches of sediment, or dams displacing communities and destroying habitats, meaning their long-term costs (both financial and environmental) can outweigh their benefits. On the other hand, soft engineering measures, being long-term, less expensive, and ecologically sensitive, allow natural processes to continue while still reducing impacts, and are more sustainable over time, though their protective effect is smaller and slower to establish, which limits their suitability where urgent protection is required. The effectiveness of either approach is also strongly shaped by the concept of Place and Power: wealthier, more developed places have the resources to implement and maintain hard measures, while less economically developed places, lacking such resources, are often limited to soft measures regardless of which is more 'effective' in the abstract. Therefore, while hard measures may appear more effective in providing immediate, forceful protection, soft measures are arguably more effective for long-term, sustainable protection; the ideal approach, as suggested, is to combine both by implementing hard measures first and using soft measures to sustain protection long-term, rather than favouring one exclusively.
rubric: Takes a clear stand (agrees to a moderate/certain extent, not fully agree or disagree)
Discusses the perspective supporting hard measures being more effective (immediate impact, extensive alteration)
Discusses the counter-perspective for soft measures (sustainability, ecological sensitivity, lower cost)

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain, using the concept of power, why more economically developed countries are better able to implement hard engineering measures than less economically developed countries. [4]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: The concept of power refers to the ability of governments to influence and effect change, including the ability to fund and implement infrastructure projects. Because hard engineering measures are costly, requiring significant financial resources and advanced technology and expertise, more economically developed countries, which possess greater financial and technological resources, are better able to implement these measures. In contrast, less economically developed countries often lack the necessary funds, technology and manpower, and so must rely on cheaper soft engineering measures instead, similar to how such countries are more able to adapt than mitigate in the context of climate change.
rubric: Defines power in relation to government ability/resources to implement measures

shortAnswer.prompt: Compare the agents and landforms associated with river and coastal systems. [4]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Both rivers and coasts are shaped by the same fundamental processes of erosion, transportation and deposition, but they differ in their driving agents and resulting landforms. Rivers are driven primarily by discharge, the volume of water flowing through the channel, which produces landforms such as floodplains, deltas and levees. Coasts, on the other hand, are driven primarily by waves, producing distinct landforms such as headlands, bays, wave-cut platforms, notches, cliffs and caves. Thus, while the underlying processes are similar, the specific agent and landforms produced differ due to the different physical setting of rivers versus coasts.

topics.title: Globalisation and Development
topics.notesHtml:
Global Forces of Change (Globalisation)

Globalisation and Development

At a glance, globalisation and development may largely seem like the same thing. However, there are vast differences between the two. For example, globalisation cannot occur within a single country and requires the interdependence of multiple countries, in contrast to development, which can occur within a single country.

Development refers to the process by which a country sees an improvement in their quality of life and standard of living, associated with increased living costs and political, social and economic reforms within a country.

Globalisation instead refers to:

  • the growing interaction, interconnectivity and interdependence of countries worldwide, among the people, companies, and governments
  • the global integration of economies, politics, products, ideas and other aspects of culture

through the:

  • aid of more rapid and widespread diffusion of information technology
  • driving force of increasing volume and variety of cross-border transactions in goods and services, and international capital flows (trade and investments)

which has led to:

  • the free movement of people
  • companies becoming multinational
  • an increase in international trade

shortAnswer.prompt: Distinguish between globalisation and development. [4]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Globalisation and development are related but distinct concepts. Development refers to the process by which a single country experiences an improvement in its quality of life and standard of living, associated with political, social and economic reforms and increased living costs, and can occur within one country alone. Globalisation, in contrast, refers to the growing interaction, interconnectivity and interdependence of multiple countries worldwide among people, companies and governments, involving the global integration of economies, politics, products, ideas and culture; unlike development, globalisation cannot occur within a single country as it inherently requires interaction between countries. Thus, the key basis of comparison is that development is an internal, single-country process, while globalisation is an inherently multi-country, interdependent process.

topics.title: Driving Forces and Aspects of Globalisation and Development
topics.notesHtml:
Driving Forces and Aspects of Globalisation

The aspects of globalisation are often seen as the driving forces of globalisation too, and vice versa. For example, the rapid and widespread diffusion of information technology has driven globalisation by allowing for increase in and ease of cross-border communications, but is also an aspect of globalisation, as a globalised country often has a strong technological network to connect itself to other countries.

However, this is not so for development — besides the key differences in the definitions of globalisation and development, there are also key differences in what the two terms entail, in their aspects and driving forces.

Aspects of Development

A developed country contains aspects such as:

  • Quality education (e.g. high literacy rate)
  • Good and affordable housing (e.g. warm and dry housing)
  • Good healthcare and medical services with higher life expectancy and decreased infant mortality
  • Clean and better food and water supply, along with proper sanitation
  • Secure employment with low unemployment rate
  • Good working conditions
  • Security in old age (financial, medical and social)
  • Good transport infrastructure and network
  • Higher GDP and GNP per capita
  • Freedom of speech
  • Gender/racial equality
  • Provision of quality recreational/entertainment services

Development is also often measured using the Human Development Index (HDI).

Driving Forces of Development

  • Social — The population, educational and health facilities play a key role in driving development. Strong educational and health facilities help to contribute to development and globalisation.
  • Infrastructure — Transport and technological infrastructure is critical to development. Good transport infrastructure ensures accessibility and ease of movement of goods and services for development and globalisation.
  • Natural Endowment — The presence of abundant and accessible natural resources and raw materials, with the infrastructure to appropriately utilise such resources, makes a country attractive for, and aids it in, development and globalisation. The presence of smooth terrain can have a similar effect, while physical factors play a key role in development and globalisation, as hilly mountains, for example, make it difficult for development.
  • Political — Power plays a key role in globalisation and development, and lies in the hands of the government. Poor leadership and governance can hinder globalisation and development.
  • Economic — Economic power and the economic situation of a country play a key role in globalisation and development. A strong economy makes a country attractive for, and aids it in, development and globalisation. The economic relationship between countries can also play a role, one such relationship being the Core-Periphery Theory, used by multinational and transnational companies.

Aspects of Globalisation

While a globalised country is very often a developed country too, a developed country may not always be a globalised country. A globalised country is brought about by, and entails, the following aspects:

  • Technological — Advanced technology which supports the processes of globalisation like overseas communication, trade, transportation, logistics, etc.
  • Political — Strong political, bilateral and multilateral ties with other countries with regards to various aspects such as defence (e.g. Singapore often conducts various military exercises with Taiwan and Australia, with multiple defence pacts with other countries including the US), economic (trade with other countries), and medical (sharing of information, etc.); increased spreading and sharing of ideologies; increased presence of global organisations (e.g. the UN).
  • Socio-Cultural — Sharing of cultures and entertainment with the integration of various cultures in multiple aspects like food, dressing, services/facilities/locations, etc. (e.g. Singapore's integration of Malay, Indian, Eurasian, Western and Chinese immigrant food, culture, festivals, dressing, and services catered to them, like Chinatown and Little India). Increasing migration and tourism makes populations more unified and diversified, with more people using, adopting and consuming increasingly similar food, clothes, music and values — many of which are 'western' in origin (from North America and Europe). There is frequent, high and increased movement of people (e.g. Singapore — in 2019, there were about 2.16 million immigrants; or the US — in absolute numbers, the United States has a larger immigrant population than any other country, with 47 million immigrants as of 2015, representing 19.1% of the 244 million international migrants worldwide, and 14.4% of the U.S. population).
  • Environmental — Accessible location for the setting up of businesses of other countries and for frequent, high and increased movement of money, exchange of goods and services, and movement of people. Natural endowment ideal and attractive for globalisation (e.g. LEDCs like Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, with an abundance of natural resources). Increasing global action towards global issues and increased global agreements (e.g. Paris Agreement and Kyoto Protocol). Spread of species to other countries due to migration of animals.
  • Economic — Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) and lower tariffs with other countries (e.g. Singapore's FTAs and the India–Singapore Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement) with rapid growth in world trade and investments.

Driving Forces of Globalisation

  • Presence and growth of many multinational and transnational companies (MNCs and TNCs) established within the country, which have a global brand image and presence
  • Frequent and increased capital mobility (the movement of money), with high, frequent and increased numbers of exports and imports to and from other countries (e.g. Singapore — at the HS6 digit level, 4,257 products are exported to 220 countries and 4,307 products are imported from 221 countries; total value of exports (FOB) is US$390,332 million, while total value of imports (CIF) is US$358,975 million)
  • High number of Foreign Direct Investments which boost the economy of the country (e.g. Singapore — according to UNCTAD's World Investment Report 2020, FDI inflows rose to USD 92 billion in 2019, from USD 79 billion a year earlier; FDI stock was about USD 1.7 trillion; Singapore is the 5th largest recipient of FDI inflows in the world, after the United States, China, the Netherlands and Hong Kong)
  • Frequent, high and increased exchanges of goods and services with multiple channels of distribution and without barriers to trade like high tariffs or embargoes
  • Cheap and reduced labour cost alongside a variety of goods and services on a wider market

Other driving factors and aspects of globalisation include:

  • Market Factors — increasing global channels of distribution, the role of technology in making world markets more accessible
  • Cost Factors — the need and desire for more cost- and time-efficient processes
  • Accessibility Factors — the dramatic fall in government and trade barriers, role of technology in accelerating the flow of information
  • Competitive Factors — the search for less competitive markets and the need for market presence necessary to execute global strategies

Trade is the buying and selling of goods and services we want and need. It involves the exchange of goods and services in return for other goods and services or money. Most importantly, it varies in scale. The scale of trade has increased through time, and exchanges can now happen on a global scale.

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain three driving forces of development, using evidence to support your answer. [6]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: One driving force of development is the social factor, where population, educational and health facilities play a key role; strong educational and health facilities directly contribute to a country's development. A second driving force is infrastructure, particularly transport and technological infrastructure, which ensures accessibility and ease of movement of goods and services, both of which are necessary for development and globalisation to occur. A third driving force is natural endowment, referring to the presence of abundant and accessible natural resources and raw materials along with suitable infrastructure to utilise them, and smooth terrain; countries with hilly, mountainous terrain find development more difficult due to physical constraints on infrastructure and accessibility. Together, these social, infrastructural and physical/natural factors interact to determine how easily a country can develop.

These economic and political ties demonstrate how deeply interconnected and interdependent Singapore is with other countries, both aspects and driving forces of its globalisation.
