topics.title: Role of Transport and Technology in Globalisation
topics.notesHtml:
Role of Transport and Technology in Globalisation

Besides the aspects and driving forces of globalisation mentioned above, improvements in transport and information technology have played a key role in globalisation, and continue to be key aspects of it. Improvements in transport technology and transportation networks have made the transportation of goods, services and people further, cheaper and quicker.

Improvements in Transportation

Made the movement of people, goods and services further, cheaper and quicker (easier, more efficient) → increased interactions between countries (globalisation).

Further

  • Goods and Services: From 1993 to 2002, the average shipping distance increased by 40%.
  • People: In the 1950s, most commercial planes would fly short distances, with a range of about 2400 km. In contrast, the invention of jet aircraft like the Airbus A380 gives planes a range of up to 15700 km, more than 4 times the original distance.

Cheaper, Quicker (More time and cost efficient)

  • Goods and Services: As a result of the invention of jet aircraft, containerisation, and improvements in technology leading to mechanised loading, the movement of goods and services is now much faster.
    • Currently, due to containerisation, the use of Standard Twenty Foot Equivalent Shipping Containers allows for up to 6000 pairs of shoes to be transported in one container.
    • Improvements in shipping technology led to innovations such as the Maersk Triple E Shipping Tanker, which can carry up to 2500 more containers and has a 16% increase in capacity compared to other ships. The Maersk Triple E also reduces fuel consumption by 37%.
    • In 1956, it took up to 1 week to load a single ship. In contrast, with improvements in technology such as mechanised loading, loading times are now (2015) reduced to 5 hours.
    • The invention of jet aircraft has provided a variety of transport options. Cargo planes are faster and more time efficient than trains and ships. Jet aircraft like the A350 are also 25 to 30% more fuel efficient.
  • These have led to reduced shipping and loading times and reduced the need for multiple trips, making the movement of goods and services more time and cost efficient.
  • People: The invention of jet aircraft reduced travel time for passengers to hours, rather than days, replacing steam ships.
    • Improvements in rail technology, like the invention of the Bullet Train, now allow trains to travel at 249 mph as opposed to 124 mph, the speed of coal and steam trains in 1986.
  • These have led to reduced travel times and reduced the need for multiple trips, making the movement of goods and services more time and cost efficient.

Containerisation is a system of standardised transport that uses a common size of steel containers that can easily be transferred between different modes of transport — container ships to lorries and trains — to transport goods.

  • Dramatically sped up goods trade and reduced costs (reduced time), making consumer goods cheaper.
    • Reduced transport costs for goods by dramatically lowering the time and manpower needed, and thus the costs of 'break bulk cargo' (products that have to be loaded individually, which traditionally took 16 days in loading and unloading).
      • The process is easily mechanised, as containers are unloaded by cranes. In the past, cargo was loaded manually in crates or stacks.
      • Reduced labour costs, as fewer dockworkers are required to unload loose commodities or pack awkwardly shaped products into the hold.
    • Less time is spent when products change transport type, as the containers are intermodal (ubiquitous, standardised metal/steel boxes quickly transferable from a ship to a lorry or railway).

Improvements in Information Technology

Made the sharing of information and connections across borders easier and quicker (more efficient) → increased interactions between countries (globalisation).

Synchronous Communication

  • With the use of smartphones and internet access, along with the development of communication platforms like Google Meet, Skype and Zoom, synchronous communication has become easier and more efficient, leading to easier interactions with even greater numbers of people in real time.
    • Currently, there are 2.1 million users of Zoom.

News and Worldwide Coverage

  • News from all over the world can now reach people faster and further. People can now more easily and quickly see more about other places.
  • The development of satellite TV channels such as Sky and CNN have also provided worldwide marketing avenues for the concept and products of globalisation.

Internet of Things

  • The Internet of Things refers to the process in which devices are increasingly becoming connected to the internet. Such devices include smartphones, laptops, home entertainment systems and car systems, which has increasingly caused our world to become more interconnected. The Internet of Things is currently changing, and will continue to change, the way global businesses operate. The internet provides lower barriers of entry, lower cost, and faster and greater return on investment than any other communication channel in human history.
    • In 2017, there were over 8.4 billion devices connected to the internet, projected to increase to 13.8 billion in 2021.
  • Internet access and online databases like OneDrive and iCloud connect people across places more easily and allow for easier sharing of information.
    • From 1995 to 2015, there was a 72% increase in the world's internet access, from 13% in 1995 to 85% in 2015.
    • Currently, there are 850 million users of iCloud.
    • The internet is the fastest growing mode of communication, taking just 4 years to reach 50 million users, compared to the radio and television, which took 38 years and 13 years respectively.
    • It has been estimated that the number of internet users around the world increased from 361 million in 2000 to 3 billion in 2015. This gives a global internet penetration rate (percentage of internet users compared to total population) of 34.4%. By world region, this varied from 29% in Africa to 88% in North America.
  • Smartphones connect people to the world at the touch of their fingertips. With a smartphone, one can easily read up on news around the world or communicate with someone across the world, and even purchase something from across the world. Smartphones bring about the use of social media and internet access, platforms that allow for ease and efficiency of connections around the world.
    • There was a 148% increase in smartphone usage from 1960 to 2017 in Singapore, and a 122% increase within the same time frame in the United States. Between 2014 and 2018, there was an overall 32% increase in the world's smartphone usage.
  • Accelerating advances in Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) such as the internet, email and mobile phones have been vital to the growth of globalisation because they help multinational and transnational companies to operate throughout the world:
    • Allows management decisions and information to be instantly communicated worldwide
    • Allows for the expansion of global trade
    • Helps to more easily and quickly connect producers and customers along supply chains
    • Facilitates delivery of basic services including finance (e-banking, Visa)
    • Allows people to communicate and businesses to continue operations 24/7, across all oceans and continents
    • Doing business via digital media has become critical to an organisation's success both online and offline (e.g. the COVID-19 situation, Grab)

Limitations

Despite the role of improvements in transportation and information technology in globalisation, governments have the ability to limit this role, and its effect varies across the world.

  • The use of ICT and quality of access to broadband is very limited in the developing world, clearly inhibiting access to global markets for some countries. In 2012, less than 1 in 100 of the population of sub-Saharan Africa had a broadband internet subscription.
  • The internet is also banned in North Korea, because the government does not want its people to have access to 'western' ideas.
  • In China, the internet was very widely used by 52% of the population in 2016, but it is censored — some searches for politically sensitive topics like the Tiananmen Square protests get no results.

Time-Space Convergence

As the average speed of transportation increases, the world becomes smaller. Technology shrinks our world, and the world is effectively shrinking, given that information, goods and services can now be transferred much more quickly.

topics.title: Role of Transnational Corporations in Globalisation
topics.notesHtml:
Role of Transnational Corporations in Globalisation

A transnational corporation or company (TNC) is defined as a firm that owns, controls, has a controlling interest, foothold or power to coordinate and control productive operations in a subsidiary enterprise in one other country or more countries than where the parent company is registered, even if it does not own them, through Foreign Direct Investments (FDIs).

Through Foreign Direct Investments (FDIs), TNCs create international connections, spreading globalisation.

Growth in the size and number of TNCs is encouraged by the creation of trade blocs, removing international barriers, and changing government policies to encourage...

flashcards.q: What is a transnational corporation (TNC)?
flashcards.a: A firm that owns, controls, has a controlling interest, foothold or power to coordinate and control productive operations in a subsidiary enterprise in one or more countries other than where the parent company is registered, even without ownership, often through FDIs.

flashcards.q: Through what mechanism do TNCs create international connections?
flashcards.a: Foreign Direct Investments (FDIs).

flashcards.q: What encourages the growth in size and number of TNCs?
flashcards.a: The creation of trade blocs, removing international barriers, and changing government policies.

flashcards.q: How do TNCs spread globalisation?
flashcards.a: By creating international connections through FDIs, spreading interconnectivity/interdependence between the parent country and host countries.

shortAnswer.prompt: Define a transnational corporation (TNC) and explain how TNCs contribute to globalisation. [4]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: A transnational corporation (TNC) is a firm that owns, controls, or has a controlling interest, foothold or power to coordinate and control productive operations in a subsidiary enterprise in one or more countries other than where the parent company is registered, even if it does not fully own the subsidiary, typically achieved through Foreign Direct Investments (FDIs). shortAnswer.prompt: Explain what factors encourage the growth in size and number of transnational corporations (TNCs). [4]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: The growth in size and number of TNCs is encouraged by several factors: the creation of trade blocs, which link multiple countries' economies together and make it easier for firms to operate and expand across member countries; the removal of international barriers, such as tariffs, which reduces the cost and difficulty of operating subsidiaries abroad; and changing government policies, which can create more favourable conditions (e.g. incentives, eased regulations) for TNCs to establish and expand their overseas operations.

topics.title: Transnational Corporations (TNCs) and Globalisation
topics.notesHtml:
TNCs and Globalisation

Economic liberalisation, including removing capital controls and legal restrictions, and creating Special Economic Zones (SEZs), has enabled the growth of transnational corporations (TNCs). TNCs influence every aspect of our lives, from the socio-cultural aspects of what we eat, wear, use and see, to the economic aspects.

These firms tend to be global brands that sell in multiple countries. They often have factories in countries that are less economically developed (LEDCs) due to a variety of reasons, while their main offices are situated in more economically developed countries (MEDCs).

Examples of TNCs (MNCs)

  • McDonald's, Coca-Cola and Apple.
  • Wal-Mart Stores had a 2016 turnover of $482 billion (equivalent to Poland's GDP) and 2,300,000 employees.
  • Nike: global headquarters in Beaverton, Oregon, USA. Employs more than 700,000 contract workers in over 700 factories worldwide, including 124 plants in China, 73 in Thailand, 35 in South Korea and 34 in Vietnam. More than 75% of the workforce is based in Asia. Nike has 542 factories situated across 42 countries.

Placing factories in other countries relies on the economic processes of outsourcing and offshoring.

ProcessOffshoringOutsourcing
DefinitionGetting work done in a different country by moving part of one's company to another area — an extension of your own company in a different countryEmploying another company to help with, or farming out, a particular aspect of the operation to another company or external organisation on the basis of a contract
BenefitsCheaper operational costs due to cheaper labour/land in another area, and faster working times due to a global talent pool; better availability of skilled people, taking advantage of expertise in that area so work can be done faster through a global talent poolSame benefits: cheaper operational costs and faster working times/access to skilled global talent
RisksRisk of employment issues and constant criticism of transferring jobs to other countries; geopolitical risks, language differences and poor communication, etc.Risk of misaligned interests of clients and vendors; increased reliance on third parties (if third parties are at risk, the company is too); risk of lack of in-house knowledge and oversight of critical (though not necessarily core) business operations, etc.

flashcards.q: What is a Transnational Corporation (TNC)?
flashcards.a: A firm that is often a global brand selling in multiple countries, typically with factories in LEDCs and main offices in MEDCs.

flashcards.q: What economic processes have enabled the growth of TNCs?
flashcards.a: Economic liberalisation, including removing capital controls and legal restrictions, and creating Special Economic Zones (SEZs).

flashcards.a: A 2016 turnover of $482 billion (equivalent to Poland's GDP) and 2,300,000 employees.

flashcards.a: Beaverton, Oregon, USA.

flashcards.q: How many contract workers and factories does Nike employ worldwide?
flashcards.a: More than 700,000 contract workers in over 700 factories worldwide.

flashcards.q: How many Nike factories are in China, Thailand, South Korea and Vietnam?
flashcards.a: 124 plants in China, 73 in Thailand, 35 in South Korea and 34 in Vietnam.

flashcards.q: What percentage of Nike's workforce is based in Asia?
flashcards.a: More than 75%.

flashcards.q: Across how many countries does Nike have factories, and how many factories in total?
flashcards.a: 542 factories across 42 countries.

flashcards.q: Define offshoring.
flashcards.a: Getting work done in a different country by moving part of one's own company to another area — an extension of the company in a different country.

flashcards.q: Define outsourcing.
flashcards.a: Employing another company to help with, or farming out, a particular aspect of operations to another company/external organisation on a contract basis.

flashcards.q: What are the benefits of offshoring/outsourcing?
flashcards.a: Cheaper operational costs due to cheaper labour/land, faster working times, and access to a global talent pool/expertise.

flashcards.q: What is a risk specific to offshoring?
flashcards.a: Risk of employment issues and criticism for transferring jobs abroad, plus geopolitical risks and language/communication differences.

flashcards.q: What is a risk specific to outsourcing?
flashcards.a: Risk of misaligned interests between clients and vendors, increased reliance on third parties, and loss of in-house knowledge/oversight.

choices: Employment issues and criticism of transferring jobs to other countries

quiz.explanation: The notes list 'increased reliance on third parties (if third parties are at risk, the company is too)' as a risk of outsourcing, which this scenario directly illustrates.

quiz.question: Nike's notes state it has 542 factories across 42 countries, including 124 plants in China, 73 in Thailand, 35 in South Korea, and 34 in Vietnam. Based on these figures, how many of Nike's factories are located in the other 38 countries?
quiz.explanation: 124 + 73 + 35 + 34 = 266 factories accounted for in those four countries; 542 - 266 = 276 factories are in the remaining countries.

shortAnswer.prompt: With reference to the data given on Nike (700,000 contract workers, 700+ factories, 124 in China, 73 in Thailand, 35 in South Korea, 34 in Vietnam, >75% workforce in Asia), describe the distribution of Nike's manufacturing workforce. [4]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Nike's manufacturing is heavily concentrated in Asia, with more than 75% of its 700,000-strong contract workforce based there, across 700 factories in 42 countries. Within Asia, China has the largest cluster with 124 plants, followed by Thailand (73), South Korea (35) and Vietnam (34), showing that East and Southeast Asian countries dominate Nike's production base, likely due to cheap labour and land in these LEDCs/NICs.
rubric: Gives a general statement/trend (heavy concentration in Asia, >75% of workforce)
Uses specific data given (124 China, 73 Thailand, 35 South Korea, 34 Vietnam)
Notes China as the largest cluster (anomaly/highest)
Links to reason (e.g. cheaper labour in these countries) without over-explaining (describe, not explain)

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain why TNCs choose to use offshoring and outsourcing when locating their operations. [6]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: TNCs use offshoring and outsourcing mainly to reduce operational costs, as labour and land are cheaper in other countries (e.g. LEDCs), increasing profit margins. They also gain access to a global talent pool, allowing faster working times and taking advantage of expertise in a particular area that may not exist domestically. For example, Nike outsources/offshores production to over 700 factories across 42 countries, including 124 plants in China, to take advantage of cheaper labour costs and specialised garment/footwear manufacturing expertise in Asia, increasing efficiency and profitability.
rubric: Point 1: cheaper operational costs (cheaper labour/land) with explanation
Point 2: faster working times/access to global talent pool and expertise with explanation
Point 3: (optional third point) risk-aware nuance or further economic reasoning
Uses a specific, detailed example with numbers (e.g. Nike's 124 factories in China)
Begins with general statement, ends with concluding link back to question

topics.title: Global Industrial Shift
topics.notesHtml:
Global Industrial Shift

Despite the risks of offshoring/outsourcing, TNCs continue to place factories in LEDCs, resulting in global industrial shift — a trend where there is a global shift in the location of large-scale manufacturing plants.

It is an effect of the role of TNCs in driving globalisation and increasing foreign direct investment in:

  • Newly industrialising countries (NICs) – countries that started industrialising in the 1960s, e.g. the 4 Asian Tigers: South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Hong Kong.
  • Recently industrialising countries (RICs) – countries that started industrialising in the 1980s, e.g. the Philippines, Indonesia and Cambodia.

Reasons manufacturing shifted from MEDCs to LEDCs

  • Attractiveness of LEDCs as areas of lower cost of production due to cheap and flexible labour and lower transportation costs — reduces manufacturing cost and increases profit.
  • High labour costs in MEDCs.
  • Larger consumer market in LEDCs due to larger population.
  • Development in transportation encouraging companies to set up factories worldwide.
  • Incentives from LEDC governments (tax incentives, tax deductions, tax-free zones) so TNCs pay less tax and gain more profit.
  • Presence of cheap raw materials, land and natural resources.
  • Few/no barriers in LEDCs – fewer trade barriers and laws not enforced by government:
    • Labour laws – no labour unions, workers have no rights, easy to exploit and cheaper; workers are overworked and underpaid with longer hours, increasing yield and profit.
    • Health and safety regulations – fewer regulations due to lack of education, often not enforced, reducing costly management needs and lowering manufacturing costs.
    • Land laws – companies can exploit and evict locals/farmers to use land without paying for it.
    • Environmental laws – companies can pollute land and water without resistance, saving on waste management costs.

Advantages for LEDCs

Employment

Setting up factories requires workers, generating more jobs and better/new job opportunities with better income. Better income increases purchase of goods and services, widening the customer base; local businesses benefit, expand and create more jobs, generating more revenue and wealth (multiplier effect).

Education and Training

TNCs invest in training and skills development to improve workforce productivity; some skills are transferable to other industries, increasing skills and expertise for LEDC workers. Global industrial shift and more efficient production leads to increased revenue for business and country, and increased income tax and corporation tax revenue, which can finance investment in education and training or fund state education (leading to more skilled workers and more income in future).

Poverty Reduction

The World Bank defines extreme poverty as an income of less than $1.25 per day (2005). Since 1990, 1 billion people have been lifted out of extreme poverty, primarily due to global shift, which provides jobs for even low-skilled workers. Some 600 million Chinese were lifted out of poverty between 1992 and 2015.

Wages

Factory work provides a reliable, regular wage, since subsistence farming income is vulnerable to weather and disease. Low wages of $2–3 per day are still double or triple existing rural income.

Investment in Infrastructure

TNC investment develops transport infrastructure (roads, railways), service infrastructure (electricity, water supply, sanitation) and public services (healthcare, education), because setting up TNCs requires initial investment in ports, airports, roads, water and electricity supply, sewers, waste management and sanitation systems. For example, China built 11,000 km of new motorways in 2015 alone.

Disadvantages for LEDCs

Social Problems

Exploitation of the labour force with long hours and low pay; poor working conditions compromise workers' health and safety, leading to poor living/working conditions or health issues.

Loss of Productive Land

Construction of factories, infrastructure and worker housing occupies land previously used for agriculture, often the flat coastal or flood-plain land with the highest fertility and productive potential. Air and water pollution from industrial activity can render more agricultural land unusable.

Environmental Impacts

Industrial activity produces serious air and water pollution. Resource extraction creates environmental pressure elsewhere, e.g. deforestation for timber (Togo lost 60% of its forested area since 1990) or mining expansion.

Impact on Natural Resources

Pressure on natural resources, especially water supply, as new factories and offices increase demand. Manufacturing and construction of supporting infrastructure/housing creates demand for additional raw material inputs.

Impact on the Economy of the LEDC

Globalisation (with improvements in IT and transportation) inevitably impacts small-scale and local businesses heavily due to reduced labour costs from larger competitors. Global interdependence also means a heavier impact if one country fails, as other countries fail too. Profits of globalisation are often distributed unfairly to the rich while the poor are exploited, jobs threatened, and the environment heavily impacted by increased movement of people and production. Advertising by large TNCs may undermine local culture, and large TNCs may monopolise markets, hindering local startups/brands unable to compete.

See also: A Nike Case Study (referenced in the notes).

topics.title: Impact of Globalisation on Resources (Overview)
topics.notesHtml:
Impact of Globalisation on Resources

To consider the impact of globalisation on the Earth's resources, one must consider:

  1. How does globalisation affect resource availability and consumption?
  2. How does global pressure on resources affect the future security of places?
  3. What are the possibilities for managing resources sustainably?

Globalisation has resulted in accelerated consumption of resources. To ensure the survival of humans, sustainable development is required.

Sustainable Development refers to "meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs". Governments need to make bold moves for the future of resources and appreciate that social, economic and environmental sustainability are linked. Sustainable development also requires integrated decision making.

Globalisation is both a cause and a solution to resource issues — on one hand resulting in an imbalance in supply and demand, while on the other, providing solutions through improvements in technology.

It is important to understand the relationship between resources, namely food, energy and water.

topics.title: Food and Globalisation
topics.notesHtml:
Food

Globalisation affects the nature of the food supply chain, altering the quantity, type, cost and desirability of foods available for consumption. Large corporations (TNCs) are usually engaged in agribusiness, which affects the food supply chain — the majority of resources from agriculture are produced by these commercial food businesses.

Currently, TNCs like Walmart, and especially the Big 10 (Associated British Foods (ABF), Coca-Cola, Danone, General Mills, Kellogg, Mars, Mondelez, Nestlé, PepsiCo and Unilever), control 80% of food exports.

Increasing Demand

Food Consumption Patterns in LEDCsFood Consumption Patterns in MEDCs
Large increase in consumption of meat, eggs and fish in LEDCs such as China due to increase in wealth. Demand for livestock (cows, pigs, sheep, chickens) has increased since the 1960s due to rising income.People in MEDCs such as the USA consume a higher amount of meat, eggs and fish, but the rate of increase is smaller. People in MEDCs are consuming less red meat as this has been linked to health problems such as obesity and heart disease.

Consumption of fruits and vegetables has increased for both MEDCs and LEDCs, due to rising incomes in LEDCs and efforts of international organisations such as the World Health Organization and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN promoting their consumption. A significant amount of fruit and vegetables in a diet is believed to reduce the risk of diseases such as heart disease, cancer and diabetes.

Reasons for changing consumption

  • Rising incomes give people access to foods that were previously unaffordable.
  • Western diets are seen as more modern and fashionable, so eating meat and fast food becomes aspirational for upwardly mobile people.
  • As economic development occurs, trade links develop and a greater range of western and other foreign foods becomes available.
  • Rising farm productivity makes some foods more affordable, widening access to a growing middle class:
    • Technological changes have increased mechanisation on farms — machinery lets farmers plough and harvest much more quickly.
    • Purchased inputs such as pesticides and chemical fertilisers increase yields by removing competing plants/insects and boosting nutrients.
    • Improved spatial integration through construction of roads and railways enables farmers to transport produce cheaply to more markets, increasing sales and profits.

Issue: Imbalance in Food Supply and Demand

Globalisation results in an increase in income, unequal between LEDCs and MEDCs, leading to a change in global food consumption patterns. At the same time, globalisation has increased the disparity between rich and poor due to socio-economic factors (e.g. core-periphery theory). An increase in wealth has led to an increase in food supply in MEDCs, while a decrease in wealth has led to a decrease in food supply in LEDCs, creating an imbalance in supply and demand of food.

This imbalance is also caused by:

  • Food waste – a supply chain increases the chances of food wastage (taking more than needed and throwing away excess). From distributors to retailers, the sorting process increases wastage as imperfect food is often discarded.
  • Food loss – due to natural disasters around the world (a decrease in crop yield from damaged or destroyed crops), food loss is on the rise. The process of transporting and storing food in the supply chain also increases food loss, especially in LEDCs which lack infrastructure and skills to properly store/transport food or cope with natural disasters.

These factors result in an imbalance in the supply and demand of food in LEDCs and MEDCs, leading to food shortage and insecurity. Food security, as defined by the United Nations, means all countries should have sufficient, safe and nutritious food at all times.

topics.title: Managing Food Shortage
topics.notesHtml:
Managing Food Shortage

GM (Genetically Modified) Crops

Food derived from crops with genetic make-up modified to create desired qualities (e.g. more resistance), by taking desirable genetic traits from other organisms and transplanting them into plants/animals. Common GM foods include potatoes, corn, soya beans and tomatoes.

Strengths:

  • Some GM crops produce higher output than non-GM crops (e.g. Super Rice, a type of GM rice, produces double the output of normal rice); farmers can earn more income selling excess produce to overseas markets.
  • GM crops more resistant to pests, e.g. Bt corn — a bacterium (Bt), a natural pesticide, is inserted into the corn plant so it suffers less insect damage, increasing farmer output.
  • Some GM crops stay fresh longer, letting farmers sell to markets further away and earn more money to invest in their farms.
  • GM food can withstand greater variations in weather/climate and tolerate more saline water, allowing cultivation on land once thought unsuitable for farming, producing more food for the world.
  • Improved nutritional value of food.

Limitations:

  • Fear of potential health risks/unknown consequences of consuming unnatural GM food, including allergies; the EU bans import/cultivation of most GM crops, and countries like Zambia reject GM food imports fearing health impacts. (e.g. lectin, a protein from beans, used in potatoes to prevent aphid attacks, but some people are allergic to lectin.)
  • GM crops are limited in availability and affordability; generally only farmers in MEDCs or richer LEDC farmers have the means and capital to grow them, unlike poor farmers.

Green Revolution

The application of science and modern agricultural techniques to increase agricultural productivity, including breeding high-yield varieties (HYVs) of grains, effective use of pesticides, and improved fertilisation, irrigation, mechanisation and soil conservation techniques.

Strengths:

  • High Yielding Varieties (HYVs) – crops specially bred/selected through cross-breeding to produce higher output than natural species. HYV IR8 rice was produced in India in the 1960s, significantly reducing food shortage as it was more resistant to drought and disease, had a shorter growing period, doubling/tripling crop yield per year.
  • Other innovations: central pivot irrigation (mechanised irrigation with pipes/overhead sprinklers on wheeled towers moving around a central point), and combined harvesters, weeders and ploughs (farm mechanisation). Yields are twice to four times greater than traditional varieties, as irrigation can be done more easily and quickly over wider areas, allowing larger farms.
  • Increased crop yield led to increased farming income, allowing purchase of machinery, better seeds, fertilisers and pesticides, contributing to even greater yield increases. The diet of rural communities is now more varied due to spread of different foods/crops to different countries.

Limitations:

  • High inputs of fertiliser and pesticide required, costly economically and environmentally; rural indebtedness has risen sharply in some areas.
  • HYVs require more weed control and are often more susceptible to pests and diseases.
  • Middle and higher-income farmers have benefited much more than low-income majority, widening the income gap in rural communities.
  • Mechanisation has increased rural unemployment.
  • Salinisation has increased along with expansion of irrigated area.

Agribusiness

Strengths:

  • Large-scale food production by TNCs makes food available to areas without sufficient supply, as TNCs export to hunger-stricken countries.
  • TNCs may sell food more cheaply to local consumers due to economies of scale.
  • Foods produced by TNCs often have preservatives, increasing shelf life so consumers do not suffer food shortages from poor storage or perishability (reducing food loss).
  • TNCs give consumers the opportunity to make food choices according to preference.

Limitations:

  • Many poor farmers are unable to compete: TNCs use land for large factories, taking away farming land from locals/farmers, denying power to cultivate food for domestic consumption, possibly leading to food shortages.
  • TNCs may encourage growing non-food cash crops rather than food crops, limiting consumer food choice and possibly decreasing food supply.
  • TNCs may gain control of the supply of seed for basic crops; seed may then be priced beyond the means of the average farmer, or require unaffordable investment in infrastructure/equipment for high yields.

topics.title: Water and Globalisation
topics.notesHtml:
Water

Globally, water consumption is not equal. This imbalance in demand and supply, along with growing demand, results in the issue of water shortage.

Reasons for unequal water consumption

  1. MEDC consumption > LEDC consumption:
    MEDCLEDC
    >1600 cubic metres of water a year (average person in North America); up to 800 litres per person per day<200 cubic metres a year (average person in sub-Saharan Africa); only 10 litres per person per day
  2. Temporal and seasonal differences: In India, most renewable water resources arrive during the three-month monsoon period, when 70–95% of annual precipitation occurs.
  3. Large differences in precipitation between continents, regions, countries, and within countries. Regionally, South and Central America with the Caribbean is the wettest continent, averaging more than 1600mm/year, compared to North America (637mm/year), Africa (677mm/year) and Europe (545mm/year). Locally, Egypt has the lowest precipitation worldwide at only 51mm/year, but the Nile brings large amounts of freshwater from neighbouring countries to the south; renewable freshwater resources per person are 1900 litres/day in Egypt, much higher than in Libya (300 litres/day).

Increasing Demand

Demand for freshwater has tripled over the last 50 years as the world's population grows, increasing by 64 billion cubic metres a year. Demand grows not only for domestic water, but also from industry as countries develop, and from agriculture as irrigated farmland area increases.

On a global scale, agriculture uses the largest amount of freshwater, representing about 70% of all water withdrawal worldwide (with regional variation). The productivity of irrigated land is roughly three times greater than rain-fed land, and global food production is expected to increase by 60% from 2000 to 2030, creating a 14% increase in water demand for irrigation.

Our water footprint and virtual water footprint are also growing. The water footprint measures humanity's appropriation of freshwater in volumes consumed and/or polluted, including:

  • Amount of water used to produce each good/service we use.
  • Amount of water used for fuel.
  • Amount of water used for every process (e.g. growing rice).
  • Amount of water used for a product (e.g. a pair of jeans).

Everything we use, wear, buy, sell and eat takes water to make.

Water Scarcity

Economic Water ScarcityPhysical Water Scarcity
Water is available, but inaccessible or unusable, due to: groundwater that is expensive to extract, too costly to transport, or difficult/unable to do either; or the water supply has become polluted.Water is not available.

Industrial demand also grows as countries develop economically, while agricultural demand rises as more land becomes irrigated — irrigated land is roughly three times more productive than rain-fed land, and as global food production is expected to rise 60% from 2000 to 2030, this alone will create a 14% increase in water demand for irrigation. Additionally, our water footprint and virtual water footprint are growing, as water is used to produce nearly everything we consume, wear or use, from goods to fuel.

topics.title: Managing Water Shortage
topics.notesHtml:
Managing Water Shortage

SolutionAdvantagesDisadvantages
Rivers, lakes and other natural bodies of water – includes restoration of damaged rivers, lakes and wetlands so they can play their full and proper part in the hydrological cycleWater is naturally available and easy to access/distribute to users; dams and reservoirs can be built to further increase storage.In LEDCs these sources can become easily polluted, and if untreated can carry diseases such as cholera.
Wells and boreholesWater is naturally purified by filtration through bedrock and can exist in arid areas with limited surface water (e.g. Great Artesian Basin in Australia).Constructing wells costs money, as does extracting water through pumps; usually limited in quantity and cannot sustain large populations or agriculture.
Desalination plants / filtration technologySupply is virtually unlimited (sea water).Extremely expensive and uses a lot of energy (contributing to global warming).
Rainwater harvesting – (LEDC) people collect rain falling on roofs and store it in buckets for domestic purposes (flushing toilets, watering gardens); (MEDC) water collected in large catchment areas and reservoirsWater is usually very pure and can be consumed with limited treatment.Rain is unpredictable and storage can be difficult — not reliable and requires large catchment space.
Water condensingWater is very pure and does not require treatment; technology is inexpensive and simple.Can only provide small quantities of water.

Solutions to reduce agricultural water demand

  • Smart irrigation – traditional sprinklers and surface flow systems replaced by modern automated spray technology and advanced drip irrigation systems.
  • Hydroponics – growing crops in greenhouses that are carbon dioxide and temperature controlled, in shallow trays where they are drip-fed nutrients and water; no soil used.
  • Recycling of greywater – a low-cost option producing water for agricultural use, but not human consumption.

shortAnswer.prompt: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of desalination plants and rainwater harvesting as solutions to water shortage. [6]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Both desalination and rainwater harvesting aim to increase water supply, but differ in reliability and cost. Desalination plants offer a virtually unlimited supply since they use sea water, making them suitable for coastal areas facing physical scarcity; however, they are extremely expensive and energy-intensive, which can contribute to global warming. Rainwater harvesting, by contrast, produces very pure water requiring limited treatment, and can be done cheaply at a household level (LEDCs) or via large catchments (MEDCs); however, rainfall is unpredictable and storage can be difficult, making it unreliable and space-intensive. Overall, desalination suits large-scale, consistent supply needs, while rainwater harvesting is cheaper but less dependable.

topics.title: Energy and Globalisation
topics.notesHtml:
Energy

Due to globalisation, global energy demand is expected to grow by 30% before 2035, driven by increasing prosperity in developing countries. Traditional centres of demand are being overtaken by fast-growing emerging markets such as India and China.

Energy powers the world, allowing economies and societies to function, making it critical for life to go on. At the same time, energy moves around the world.

The energy crisis is the concern that the rate of consumption overwhelms the rate of replenishment/production of energy, making our current overreliance on fossil fuels unsustainable. If this continues, the world would eventually run out of fossil fuels, creating a shortage of energy worldwide.

The energy crisis stems from the issue of fossil fuels: more than ¾ of the world's energy supply in 2018 was from fossil fuels, meaning the world is too dependent on these sources. While fossil fuels provide effective amounts of energy, they are limited in supply and take thousands of years to replenish. They are also found almost exclusively in OPEC countries, so regional issues may cause a worldwide energy shortage. They also cause major land, air and water pollution, contributing greatly to climate change.

The supply of fossil fuels continues to dwindle, and there is an overall lack in renewable energy production, so supply of energy is unable to match growing demand, which is increasing because of:

  1. Entertainment requires energy – in developed/globalised economies, besides commuting to work, people travel to see friends, enjoy pastimes and go on holidays.
  2. Increasing use of labour-saving devices – devices like vacuum cleaners and washing machines make life easier and free up time for leisure, but require energy.
  3. Increasing desire for car ownership grows continuously worldwide.
  4. Increasing world population.
  5. Globalisation and developing industries which require even more energy to function.
  6. Poor infrastructure and wastage also leads to energy being used less effectively.

Globalisation plays a key role in this imbalance: on one hand it increases the use of technology and the production/exchange of goods and services, increasing energy demand. On the other hand, it increases interactions between countries and the possibilities of sharing ideas and resources for renewable energy, and leads to improvements in technology that could reduce demand for energy via cleaner and more efficient forms of energy or production, requiring less consumption of conventional energy.

topics.title: Managing Energy Shortage
topics.notesHtml:
Managing Energy Shortage

1. Demand Reduction

Reduction in demand for fossil fuel energy and for energy services, both contributing to reducing carbon emissions from energy use. Demand reduction helps make energy supplies more sustainable, as supply should be able to match demand into the future.

2. Increased Energy Efficiency

Reducing energy needed to perform tasks and eliminating wastage during consumption. This makes energy supply more sustainable by conserving as much energy as possible, offering a more immediate method to reduce fossil fuel use. By reducing overall energy use, fewer resources are used up and environmental effects (e.g. greenhouse gas emissions) are limited.

Homes, workplaces and transport can be designed to conserve energy:

  • Buildings can be made more sustainable, reducing energy needed for heating and lighting by installing double glazing, draught-proofing, loft insulation and cavity wall insulation to reduce heat loss, as well as features that absorb/retain the sun's energy (e.g. large south-facing windows) to provide heat and light.
  • Energy-efficient appliances, like energy-efficient boilers where a greater proportion of heat energy is used to heat water and less is lost to surroundings; use energy-saving appliances wherever possible (e.g. energy-saving light bulbs).
  • Using computers, printers and faxes that turn themselves off after a period of time instead of staying on (stand-by mode can consume nearly as much energy as being turned on permanently).
  • Changing to vehicles that need no fuel, with incentives (e.g. bicycles – employers receive tax exemptions for loaning or selling bicycles as part of the Cycle to Work scheme), and designing cars to need less fuel to run.
  • Establishing out-of-town park-and-ride schemes, investing in public transport, and introducing congestion charges – reduces fuel consumption by reducing the number of vehicles on the road (e.g. London, Singapore, Rome and Stockholm).

3. Renewable Energy

Increasingly using energy produced by renewable sources like the sun, wind or rivers. Since these can be replenished much faster than fossil fuels and produce little carbon emissions, they are a sustainable source that will never run out. Increasing renewable energy use decreases reliance on fossil fuels and increases clean energy supply.

Disadvantages include high costs, inconsistency due to changing weather/climate, and producing less energy than fossil fuels — though future scientific and technological advancements may resolve these concerns.

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain how increased energy efficiency in buildings and appliances can help manage the energy crisis. [6]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Increased energy efficiency reduces the energy needed to perform tasks and eliminates wastage, conserving energy and limiting environmental effects such as greenhouse gas emissions. Buildings can be made more energy efficient through double glazing, draught-proofing, and loft/cavity wall insulation to reduce heat loss, as well as features like large south-facing windows that absorb and retain solar heat, reducing the need for artificial heating and lighting. Appliances can also be made more efficient, such as energy-efficient boilers that direct more heat to water rather than losing it to surroundings, and computers/printers that switch off automatically instead of remaining on stand-by, which can otherwise consume nearly as much energy as being fully on. Together, these measures conserve significant amounts of energy, helping supply more sustainably match demand.
rubric: Explains the general purpose of energy efficiency (reduce energy needed, eliminate wastage)
Gives specific building examples (insulation, double glazing, south-facing windows)
Gives specific appliance/device examples (boilers, stand-by mode data)
General opening and concluding statement linking to sustainability of energy supply

shortAnswer.prompt: Evaluate the effectiveness of renewable energy as a solution to the energy crisis. [6]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Renewable energy is an effective long-term solution because sources like the sun, wind and rivers can be replenished far faster than fossil fuels and produce little carbon emissions, meaning they can theoretically supply energy indefinitely while reducing environmental damage. This directly addresses the unsustainability of fossil fuel dependence. However, its effectiveness is currently limited by high costs of technology and installation, inconsistency due to changing weather and climate conditions (e.g. solar/wind output varies), and generally lower energy output compared to fossil fuels. As such, while renewable energy offers a sustainable long-term direction, its present limitations mean it must be paired with demand reduction and efficiency measures, with future technological advances needed to fully replace fossil fuels.
rubric: Identifies strengths of renewable energy (fast replenishment, low emissions, sustainability) with reasoning
Identifies weaknesses (cost, weather inconsistency, lower output) with reasoning
Gives a balanced judgement/evaluation rather than one-sided description
Concluding statement taking a stand on overall effectiveness

topics.title: Challenges of Globalisation: Pros and Cons
topics.notesHtml:
Challenges of Globalisation

Globalisation continues to face challenges despite its various positive benefits. Below are the pros and cons across different dimensions.

Economic

Pros: Ease of trade and exchange of goods and services, leading to economic growth and strengthening of economies through increased interdependence of countries (e.g. specialised nations can work together to create cheaper goods). The US relies on India for half of its computer service imports; India's computer service exports rose from $11 billion in 1995 to almost $110 billion in 2015, with economic growth in India averaging 6.5% a year during that time (strengthening of each other's economies). LEDCs like Zambia are able to develop by reducing debt through World Bank's help. Access to newer, larger markets brings better availability of products/services, increased customer base, wider market and increased profit, strengthening the economy (less chance of shortage).

Cons: Increased vulnerability and reliance of LEDC countries – they become too dependent on wealthier countries to invest in them and are unable to function without this support system.

Socio-Economic

Pros:

  1. Increased job opportunities – Social: increase in employment/job opportunities and education (reduces unemployment), upskilling of LEDC population, providing stable and better jobs/income for a decent standard of living. Economic: more people working increases GDP and GDP per capita. E.g. TNCs provide access to a larger market and, by offshoring factories in LEDCs, provide jobs and better income for the LEDC population (reducing poverty and unemployment).
  2. Alleviation of poverty – globalisation significantly increases capital mobility; remittances (people working in MEDCs sending money to their hometown in LEDCs) have become increasingly popular, leading to improved conditions, sanitation and education over time, helping locals break the poverty cycle. E.g. $2,600,000,000 USD sent to the Philippines annually (9.7% of 2020 GDP) according to the World Bank.
  3. More efficient shipping and transportation – Social: increased ease of travel, increased access to goods/services (cheaper, faster). Economic: increased movement of people means a greater number/variety of customers and increased access to goods/services. E.g. the Boeing 747 (introduced in the 1960s) lowered the cost of international air travel, increasing tourism and business travel and reducing travel time from days to hours, replacing steam ships. Containerisation also reduced transport costs for goods by cutting the cost/time of manual loading, using standard-sized containers and mechanised loading, speeding up trade and making consumer goods cheaper.
  4. Increased sharing of information and digital exchanges across countries – Social: people can connect with friends/family in other countries with ease. Economic: businesses can have worldwide marketing avenues and connect with customers/producers faster (link to socio-political aspect).
  5. Increased development and standard of living – Social: increased development, infrastructure and access to goods/services raises standard of living. Economic: increased development (via foreign direct investment), more companies set up, increasing GDP and revenue. E.g. TNCs setting up factories in LEDCs require investment in basic services/infrastructure (water, electricity, roads), contributing to development and a more stable supply of energy and roads.

Cons: Exploitation of labour in LEDCs – underpaid and overworked workers. E.g. the setting up of TNC factories in LEDCs allows exploitation of cheaper labour due to relaxed labour laws; Nestlé, which has factories in Pakistan, reportedly uses child labour, with globalisation seeming to only benefit the rich while the government fails to protect people (Pakistanis exploited by TNCs; see also Nike case study). After workers experience health issues from poor working conditions, TNCs do not take responsibility or provide care/treatment. Most jobs provided are low-skill and do not offer much upskilling opportunity. However, some wage is better than no wage, and over time locals can send their children to school, giving them a proper education and a chance to break the poverty cycle. Finally, income disparity increases with greater extremes of inequality, and internal disparities remain.

Socio-Political

Pros: Increased ties between countries with increased access to international aid and financial support, meaning smaller/unstable LEDCs can gain more stability. Governments can learn from each other, sharing policies on managing economic, social and environmental issues. E.g. organisations such as the Red Cross can respond more swiftly to disasters with a wider network and staff willing to travel/relocate. International organisations like the UN or ASEAN allow increased interactions and sharing of political, economic, social and environmental solutions/policies. Military cooperation between countries (e.g. the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty or anti-terrorism agreements) allows greater force against international terrorist groups. The political trade agreement between Singapore and India (CECA) increases trade, strengthening both economies and alleviating unemployment and poverty. Globalisation also results in increased sharing of information across the world, allowing issues to be raised on a global stage and criticised or solved more easily through global cooperation.

Cons: Globalisation can result in the decline of the nation state and its sovereignty — TNCs with a strong foothold in a country, especially LEDCs with poor, easily corrupted governments, can influence how the country is run in ways that favour the rich and place the brunt of negative impacts on the poor. TNCs can challenge the law unchallenged (e.g. Nestlé in Pakistan reportedly uses child labour in cocoa manufacturing without being stopped by the government). Globalisation's advancement of technology also makes countries more vulnerable through the Internet of Things (e.g. cyber attacks, voting fraud, online shopping crimes causing increasing dollar losses).

Socio-Cultural

Pros: Increased access to a more diverse culture (new variety of food, movies, music, art, etc.). Global links have increased opportunities for self-development through global travel and tourism, letting more people see the world and experience new cultures. Global technologies have also reinvigorated some declining cultures. E.g. diffusion of cuisines such as American fast food chains – in 2015, McDonald's had 36,000 outlets and Starbucks 24,000 outlets worldwide. Trading of foods such as avocados and coffee: coffee originated in Ethiopia and was consumed in the Arabic region, but due to globalisation and commercial trade after the 11th century it is now a globally consumed commodity. Avocados, grown mostly in the tropical climates of Mexico, the Dominican Republic or Peru, started as a small local product but today guacamole/avocado toast is common in meals worldwide.

Socio-Environmental

Pros: Diffusion of good values of environmental conservation and human rights – global consciousness has led to greater ecological awareness. Increased food supply and crop yield (through technology development) and improved technologies for monitoring climate change. E.g. some GM food crops (like Super Rice) produce double the output of normal rice, and pest-resistant crops like Bt corn suffer less damage, letting farmers grow more and earn more (see disadvantages of GM crops above). Increased awareness and global action towards environmental issues, e.g. the Paris Agreement (signed by 195 countries) provides a framework for avoiding dangerous climate impacts by "limiting global warming to well below 2°C and pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C", with larger countries helping smaller countries meet targets; other examples include the Kyoto Protocol. Environmental cooperation between countries has helped reduce chlorofluorocarbon (CFC) emissions and slow ozone depletion, e.g. the Montreal Protocol, since which the ozone hole in Antarctica has started to recover. International power grids reduce waste by reducing excess energy produced – many European nations import/export excess electricity; e.g. Germany exported 52.5 terawatts of electricity in 2020, giving importers more accessible energy and reducing wastage for Germany.

Cons:

  1. Habitat loss and deforestation – due to the large space required for factories, producing increased greenhouse gas emissions, and extraction of raw materials/fossil fuels.
  2. Ocean pollution and acidification (70% of all freight is transported by boat) – resulting in large oil spills causing high marine life deaths and extensive damage to marine environments; shipping also destroys ocean habitats through pollution.
  3. Specialisation also harms the environment. E.g. Brazil experiences extreme deforestation due to extensive ranching and agrarian activities; overfishing in SEA due to great demand for and attractive value of selling fish reduces fish populations; Brazil's soybean production, driven by global demand, has led to destruction of land (26 million to 260 million soybean production required 23 million hectares for soybean cultivation).
  4. While TNC factories in LEDCs may help set up basic infrastructure and stable water/electricity supply, they can also cause high land pollution. E.g. in Pakistan, TNCs like Nestlé have harmed children through filthy water, and Nestlé's bottled water production and super-consumption of water for production take clean water away from locals (could also take away electricity supply); infrastructure set up may not be made accessible to the locals.

flashcards.a: The Boeing 747 lowered international air travel costs, increasing tourism/business travel and cutting travel time from days to hours; containerisation cut transport costs and time via standard-sized containers and mechanised loading, speeding up trade.

flashcards.a: Globalisation can result in decline of nation state sovereignty, as TNCs with strong footholds (especially in LEDCs with corruptible governments) can influence how a country is run, favouring the rich while burdening the poor.

flashcards.a: Diffusion of cuisines like American fast food chains (McDonald's had 36,000 outlets, Starbucks 24,000 outlets worldwide in 2015); also coffee (originally from Ethiopia) and avocados (from Mexico/Dominican Republic/Peru) becoming globally consumed.

flashcards.a: The Paris Agreement (195 countries, limiting warming to well below 2°C, pursuing 1.5°C), the Kyoto Protocol, and the Montreal Protocol (helped ozone layer recovery by reducing CFC emissions).

shortAnswer.prompt: Using the ESPN framework, explain both positive and negative socio-economic impacts of globalisation. [6]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Globalisation has generated significant socio-economic benefits, particularly increased job opportunities: TNCs offshoring factories to LEDCs provide employment and better income than before, reducing poverty and unemployment while raising GDP. Remittances have also alleviated poverty, as seen in the Philippines, where workers abroad send home $2.6 billion USD annually (9.7% of 2020 GDP), improving local conditions, sanitation and education. However, globalisation also brings negative socio-economic impacts: labour exploitation is common in LEDCs, as seen with Nestlé's reported use of child labour in Pakistan, where relaxed labour laws allow underpayment and overwork, and most jobs offered are low-skill with limited upskilling opportunity, while income disparity between rich and poor increases. Overall, while globalisation has lifted many out of poverty, it has done so unevenly, with clear exploitation risks alongside genuine gains.
rubric: Explains at least one positive socio-economic impact with example/data (jobs, remittances)
Explains at least one negative socio-economic impact with example/data (Nestlé/labour exploitation, income disparity)
Covers both positive and negative (ESPN-style balance) as required for 'impacts' questions
General opening/concluding statement linking back to the question

shortAnswer.prompt: To what extent do you agree that globalisation benefits LEDCs? Discuss with reference to economic, socio-political and environmental aspects. [6]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: This statement can be agreed to a large extent, as globalisation provides LEDCs with substantial economic and socio-political benefits, though this must be balanced against real environmental and social costs. Economically, globalisation grants LEDCs access to larger markets and increased trade, as with India's computer service exports rising from $11 billion to almost $110 billion between 1995 and 2015, alongside 6.5% annual economic growth. Socio-politically, agreements like the Singapore-India CECA and international bodies like the Red Cross provide LEDCs with stability, aid and cooperation they otherwise lack. However, it must also be acknowledged that globalisation can undermine nation state sovereignty, as TNCs may exploit weak governance in LEDCs (e.g. Nestlé's alleged use of child labour in Pakistan), and cause significant environmental harm, such as deforestation from resource extraction (e.g. Brazil's soybean expansion). On balance, while globalisation is not without serious costs, its long-term economic and socio-political gains for LEDCs generally outweigh these drawbacks.
rubric: Takes a clear stand (large/small extent) rather than fully agreeing/disagreeing
Discusses at least two perspectives/dimensions (economic and socio-political benefit) with specific data
Acknowledges a counterpoint (environmental or social cost) with example
Concludes by re-emphasising the stand with a basis of argument

topics.title: Summary of Globalisation
topics.notesHtml:
Summary of Globalisation

Globalisation is the growing interdependence of countries worldwide through the increasing volume and variety of cross-border transactions in goods and services and of international capital flows, and through the more rapid and widespread diffusion of technology. With growing interdependence between countries, they would not be as adversely affected by adverse processes, since they can receive support and information from other countries to combat these impacts.

Globalisation benefits everyone, whether equally or not, over time and varying in scale from place to place. This is not to say that LEDCs do not benefit at all from globalisation and become more vulnerable as a result.

While it may not benefit LEDCs in the short term, due to issues such as labour abuse and exploitation of natural resources, globalisation does benefit LEDCs in the long term. For example, they can grow their economy and improve relations with MEDCs as they gain access to new information and improve their own country through aspects such as public awareness, stabilising their economy and socio-political relations.

With a larger influence of globalisation over many countries, there is more reliance between MEDCs and LEDCs, which can help elevate less developed countries. There is also unison in movements and actions, such as the Paris Agreement and the Kyoto Protocol, which help with mitigation and adaptation to negative impacts that globalisation might bring.

As a result, weighing the benefits and problems of globalisation, in the long term its benefits help to stabilise the state of countries in economic, social, political and environmental aspects.

flashcards.q: How is globalisation defined in the summary?
flashcards.a: The growing interdependence of countries worldwide through increasing volume and variety of cross-border transactions in goods and services and international capital flows, and more rapid/widespread diffusion of technology.

flashcards.q: What benefit does growing interdependence bring to countries facing adverse processes?
flashcards.a: Countries are not as adversely affected since they can receive support and information from other countries to combat these impacts.

flashcards.q: Does globalisation benefit all countries equally?
flashcards.a: No — globalisation benefits everyone, but not equally, and varies in scale from place to place; this does not mean LEDCs do not benefit at all.

flashcards.q: How does globalisation's benefit to LEDCs differ in the short term versus long term?
flashcards.a: In the short term it may not benefit LEDCs due to issues like labour abuse and exploitation of natural resources, but in the long term it benefits LEDCs by growing their economy and improving relations with MEDCs.

flashcards.q: What examples of unified global action are given to mitigate globalisation's negative impacts?
flashcards.a: The Paris Agreement and the Kyoto Protocol.

flashcards.q: What is the overall conclusion on weighing globalisation's benefits and problems?
flashcards.a: In the long term, its benefits help to stabilise the state of countries in economic, social, political and environmental aspects.

quiz.question: How does the summary define globalisation?
choices: The growing interdependence of countries through cross-border transactions, capital flows and technology diffusion
The isolation of national economies from each other
quiz.explanation: This is the definition given in the summary notes.

quiz.question: According to the summary, does globalisation benefit all countries equally?
choices: No, it benefits everyone but unequally and varies by place
No, it only benefits MEDCs and never LEDCs
quiz.explanation: The notes state globalisation benefits everyone, whether equally or not, and varies in scale from place to place.

quiz.question: How does the short-term impact of globalisation on LEDCs typically differ from the long-term impact per the summary?
choices: Long term impacts are always worse than short term
Short term is always positive, long term always negative
Short term may involve labour abuse/exploitation, but long term benefits include economic growth and improved relations
There is no difference between short and long term
quiz.explanation: The summary states short-term issues like labour abuse exist, but long-term globalisation benefits LEDCs' economies and relations with MEDCs.

quiz.question: Which two agreements are cited as examples of unified action to mitigate globalisation's negative impacts?
choices: The WTO and the UN Charter
The Paris Agreement and the Kyoto Protocol
quiz.explanation: The summary cites the Paris Agreement and Kyoto Protocol as examples of unified movements/actions.

quiz.question: According to the summary, what does growing interdependence between countries allow them to do when facing adverse processes?
choices: Compete with each other to solve the problem alone
Receive support and information from other countries to help combat these impacts
quiz.explanation: The summary states that with growing interdependence, countries would not be as adversely affected by adverse processes, since they can receive support and information from other countries to combat these impacts.

quiz.question: Which two specific issues does the summary identify as reasons globalisation may not benefit LEDCs in the short term?
choices: Currency devaluation and stock market crashes
Labour abuse and exploitation of natural resources
quiz.explanation: The summary states that globalisation may not benefit LEDCs in the short term due to issues such as labour abuse and exploitation of natural resources.

quiz.question: In the long term, according to the summary, how can LEDCs benefit from globalisation?
choices: By relying solely on natural resource exports
By closing their borders to reduce foreign influence
By growing their economy and improving relations with MEDCs through access to new information and public awareness
quiz.explanation: The summary states that in the long term, LEDCs can grow their economy and improve relations with MEDCs as they gain access to new information and improve their own country through aspects like public awareness and stabilising economic and socio-political relations.

quiz.question: Based on the summary's overall reasoning, which statement best explains why increased reliance between MEDCs and LEDCs can help 'elevate' less developed countries?
choices: Because international law requires MEDCs to transfer wealth directly to LEDCs
Because increased reliance gives LEDCs access to support and information from MEDCs, consistent with the summary's point that interdependence softens the impact of adverse processes
Because reliance removes any need for LEDCs to develop their own economies
Because MEDCs stop trading with each other once they rely on LEDCs
quiz.explanation: This connects two points in the summary: greater reliance between MEDCs and LEDCs can elevate LEDCs, and this works because interdependence generally lets countries receive support and information from others to combat adverse impacts — not through legal wealth transfers or reduced self-development.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT part of the summary's concluding assessment of globalisation's long-term impact?
choices: It helps stabilise countries socially and politically
It guarantees every country benefits equally and immediately
quiz.explanation: The summary concludes that in the long term globalisation's benefits help stabilise countries economically, socially, politically and environmentally — but it explicitly states benefits vary in scale from place to place and are realised 'over time,' not equally or immediately for every country.

shortAnswer.prompt: To what extent do you agree that globalisation's long-term benefits outweigh its short-term costs for LEDCs? [6]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: This statement can be agreed to a large extent, as while globalisation may not benefit LEDCs immediately due to issues such as labour abuse and exploitation of natural resources, it does provide long-term benefits by growing their economies and improving relations with MEDCs. Growing interdependence between countries means LEDCs are not as adversely affected by negative processes alone, since they can receive support and information from other nations, and unified international movements such as the Paris Agreement and Kyoto Protocol help mitigate and adapt to globalisation's negative impacts. However, it must also be acknowledged that short-term costs are real and can be severe for the populations experiencing them directly. On balance, weighing the benefits and problems, globalisation's long-term effect is to help stabilise countries economically, socially, politically and environmentally, justifying general agreement with the statement.
rubric: Takes a clear stand (large/small extent)
Explains long-term benefits (economic growth, improved relations, stabilisation) referencing the notes
Acknowledges short-term costs (labour abuse, resource exploitation) as a counterpoint
Concludes with a basis of argument (long-term vs short-term) linking back to the statement

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain how increased interdependence between countries, resulting from globalisation, helps to manage adverse global processes. [4]
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Globalisation increases interdependence between countries through greater cross-border transactions, capital flows and technology diffusion. This means that when adverse processes occur, countries are not as badly affected on their own, since they can receive support and information from other countries to help combat these impacts. This is reinforced by unified global movements such as the Paris Agreement and the Kyoto Protocol, through which countries work together on mitigation and adaptation to shared negative impacts of globalisation.
rubric: Defines/references growing interdependence via globalisation
Explains that countries can receive support/information from others due to interdependence
Gives example of unified action (Paris Agreement/Kyoto Protocol)
Concluding link back to how this manages adverse processes
